articles.title: Will Four-Way Test help Pia Cayetano feel less pressured as senator-judge?
articles.summary: An emotional Senator-judge Pia Cayetano tells the impeachment court's amici curiae — retired Supreme Court justices — that she 'genuinely didn't know what to do' as her fellow minority senators were…

blocks.text: PIA CAYETANO. Senator-judge Pia Cayetano at Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial on September 16, 2026.
Senate of the Philippines

An emotional Senator-judge Pia Cayetano tells the impeachment court's amici curiae — retired Supreme Court justices — that she 'genuinely didn't know what to do' as her fellow minority senators were being slapped with cases left and right

Senator-judge Pia Cayetano took the Senate impeachment court’s discussion on the 16-vote threshold in a slightly different direction on Wednesday, September 16, raising concerns about the “pressure” she said senator-judges are facing in the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

While her fellow senator-judges largely focused their questions on the constitutional and legal implications of the two-thirds voting requirement, Cayetano used her interjection to speak about what she described as threats to her liberty and her right to speak.

“I think my timing is best that I ask now was because the question was asked: Is there pressure on senator-judges that would basically have the effect of this threshold mechanism that is being changed, eh maaapektuhan ’yun (it will be affected),” Cayetano said.

The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday heard from retired Supreme Court justices — three of them former chief justices — serving as amici curiae or “friends of the court,” on whether the 16-vote threshold should be observed despite the absence of several senators at the trial.

Retired chief justices Artemio Panganiban and Reynato Puno and retired justice Adolfo Azcuna appeared before the court, while retired chief justice Hilario Davide Jr. submitted a memorandum. The four were asked to advise the court on the interpretation of the constitutional requirement of a two-thirds vote of “all the Members of the Senate.”

In her interjection, Cayetano underscored the circumstances of several senator-judges — minority senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada who are detained over separate plunder charges, and Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa who has been in hiding amid an International Criminal Court arrest warrant against him.
Senator Loren Legarda is also on medical leave abroad.

In her case, Cayetano said she went to Singapore to “support a national team” only to learn that National Bureau of Immigration chief Melvin Matibag was supposedly “making statements that make it appear that I’m a common fugitive.”
“Na-monitor niya kung nasaan ako at meron siyang information kung anong araw ako babalik (He monitored where I am and he had information on the date of my return). Am I a fugitive?” said Cayetano.

“I will tell you all now. Am I pressured? I am. I am. I fear for my liberty. Even in the Senate, we have a colleague na walang katapusan, tantanan kami (who has been at us without end). I fear for my right to speak,” she added.

Matibag had talked about Pia and Alan Peter Cayetano’s Singapore trip and their date of return in response to reporters’ questions in a media interview. The NBI chief himself said in the same interview that he saw nothing wrong with the senator-siblings’ trip.

At the trial on Wednesday, Cayetano told Azcuna that she “genuinely [doesn’t] even know what to do” as her colleagues in the Senate minority had been slapped with cases left and right. She also shared that her staff, Monica Mitra, had been subpoenaed in connection with the investigation into the 2019 SEAGames cauldron.
“Hindi pa ho ba pressure ‘yun, Justice Azcuna?” she asked. (Is that not pressure, Justice Azcuna?)

Azcuna replied: “I think it’s not for me to judge the circumstances of that particular case. I can only reiterate the premise of my submission that the reason for the threshold is to protect the Senate from artificial and partisan moves to prevent justice from being done.”

He added: “I think perhaps we can apply the four-way test of the Rotary to your problem: Is it the truth? Is it fair? Is it beneficial to all concerned? Will it promote friendship and goodwill? I always use that test in problematic situations. So I think it will be a good place to apply it to your case.”
Cayetano smiled and said that she was aware of the Four-Way Test as her father — the late senator Renato Cayetano — was a Rotarian.

Did Azcuna’s advice ease some pressure that Cayetano felt? She eventually withdrew her question, admitting she had become emotional. “I withdraw my question. I did not mean to ask it that way. I’m very emotional about this issue. The question I meant to ask is exactly how you answered it,” she said.
Rotarians and non-rotarians alike will probably also counsel the good senator and tell her: if there is no wrongdoing whatsoever, there is nothing to fear or feel pressured about. – Rappler.com

articles.title: LA homelessness non-profit workers arrested over alleged corruption and bribes
articles.summary:
Pair accused of misappropriating millions in taxpayer dollars as Trump officials target alleged fraud in blue states

Federal law enforcement officers have

blocks.text: Federal law enforcement officers have arrested two employees of California-based homelessness non-profits on corruption charges, alleging that they misappropriated millions in taxpayer dollars.

The US justice department has arrested Michael Young, a founder of the Culver City-based nonprofit Home At Last, and Lakiya Malone, an employee of the Los Angeles-based Special Service for Groups. The two are expected to appear in court on Wednesday.

Young is charged with wire fraud in a scheme to embezzle more than $7.5m from contracts with Los Angeles county and other publicly funded agencies, which he used to open a high-end restaurant, nightclub and bingo hall.
Malone is charged with taking more than $180,000 in bribes and kickbacks from the director of another homelessness non-profit, Alexander Soofer, who has agreed to plead guilty in a separate case.

The justice department is also seeking to arrest Donye Mitchell, the CEO of the Los Angeles-based nonprofit The Big Blue Umbrella. Mitchell is charged with wire fraud in a case that alleges he fraudulently obtained $1.2m in public grant funding, which he allegedly used for personal expenses, including his own bail bonds, credit card debt and PlayStation charges

“My message to every fraudster who steals from the vulnerable is clear: we will track you down, bring charges where the evidence leads, and work relentlessly to reclaim every taxpayer dollar you stole,” said assistant attorney general Colin M McDonald of the National Fraud Enforcement Division.

The investigation was led by the homeless fraud and corruption taskforce, which US attorney Bill Essayli formed last year to “investigate fraud, waste, abuse, and corruption involving funds allocated toward the eradication of homelessness within the seven-county jurisdiction of the central district of California”.
Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass said in a Wednesday statement: “My administration has zero tolerance for fraud – period.

“Any misuse of taxpayer funds meant to help unhoused Angelenos should be met with the full force of the law. We appreciate the efforts of the Department of Justice in protecting public funds and working towards recovering dollars meant to serve Angelenos experiencing homelessness.”
The arrests come amid growing Trump administration-backed efforts to root out “fraud” in blue states, such as California.

In April, Donald Trump named JD Vance his “fraud czar”, with a focus on investigating “those blue states where crooked Democrat politicians … have had a ‘free for all’ in the unprecedented theft of taxpayer money”. Months prior, he froze federal childcare funding to Minnesota over accusations of such fraud, and halted more than a quarter-billion dollars in Medicaid funds to the state as part of efforts to ensure it was a “good steward of the American people’s tax money”.

This summer, the Trump administration suspended federal funding to Los Angeles’s homelessness agency, Lahsa, pending an investigation citing allegations of fraud. At the time, about 8% of Lahsa’s budget came from federal funding.
And earlier this week, 12 people in southern California were charged with fraudulently collecting $10m in government childcare payments, despite allegedly caring for few or no children.

“If you fail the taxpayer, if you fail our cities, if you fail our shared mission of ending homelessness, there will be consequences and we will cut you off,” housing and urban development secretary Scott Turner said at a press conference.

articles.title: High-tech dreams, low-tech reality of the Luzon Economic Corridor
articles.summary: Despite all the high-tech rhetoric, only 0.1% of the Luzon Corridor’s projects is in advanced manufacturing and 1% in digital connectivity

blocks.text: Part 1: Billions on paper: How much of Luzon Corridor’s $20-B pipeline will become real?Second of 2 parts

In the future that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. sold to a ballroom of foreign investors, the Luzon Economic Corridor was a dreamland of artificial intelligence, advanced computing, semiconductor research, and higher value manufacturing.

Filipino engineers would help design and build the technologies of the future. New Clark City would become a hub for semiconductors and AI. The Philippines, fresh off its title as an upper-middle income country, would finally have a chance to move up the value chain instead of remaining stuck in the basement.

Beyond the hotel doors, however, the dream was already meeting resistance — resistance that would soon spill into the lobby and make clear that not everyone was buying into this future. We’ll come back to that. For now, Marcos was still busy pitching it.

“We are also building the digital foundations of a modern economy,” the President told the inaugural Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) Investment Forum. “We are expanding secure connectivity and advanced computing infrastructure, strengthening cybersecurity, and establishing safeguards for the responsible use of AI.”
It was time, he said, for the Philippines to level up its role in global semiconductor and electronics production.

“We want our country to help design and build the solutions that will shape our future,” he said. “The Philippines has long been a trusted participant in global semiconductor and electronics production. We are now moving further into design, research, engineering, and other high-value activities.”

US Ambassador Lee Lipton pedalled the same electric promises, saying Washington and Manila were pursuing in New Clark City “an ambitious idea to attract investment to semiconductors, AI, and trusted technologies,” industries he said that would “shape the future for Filipinos and the free world.”
The problem is that the investment pipeline on offer today looks very different.

Rappler put that disconnect to Finance Secretary Frederick Go, the man with the herculean job of courting foreign investment and reviving a sluggish economy, and perhaps the person best placed to explain how the government plans to turn the rhetoric into reality.
Go didn’t dispute the gap. His answer, in essence, was that the Philippines first had to earn its place.

“Advanced manufacturing, electronics, AI related, and future technologies is one of our major goals,” Go told Rappler on Friday, September 11. “It won’t be handed to us on a silver platter. We have to work hard to deserve it and become a global player in these industries.”
For now, the LEC dealbook looks much more like an infrastructure program than a high-tech industrial one.
Of its 31 detailed investment opportunities, 17 are in transport and logistics, seven in energy, four in digital connectivity, one in water, and only two in advanced manufacturing.

Those two are a proposed pharmaceutical manufacturing, testing, and distribution hub in Clark and a $20-million to $25-million (P1.26-billion to P1.57-billion)* expansion of a Pampanga factory producing insulated panels for cold storage, logistics, and cleanrooms.

“Neither involves semiconductors, AI, or anything close to the high-technology supply chains the US and Philippine governments keep invoking,” Rappler resident economist JC Punongbayan said about both advanced manufacturing projects.
The disparity is even starker when measured in dollars.

At the upper end of the ranges disclosed in the dealbook, Rappler tallied about $20.7 billion (P1.30 trillion) in opportunity values. Transport and logistics account for around $13.76 billion (P864.5 billion), while energy contributes another $6.70 billion (P421.0 billion). Together, the two sectors make up almost 99% of the pipeline with disclosed values.

That leaves barely a sliver of the disclosed pipeline for the sectors supposedly at the heart of the government’s future-ready pitch — around 0.1% for advanced manufacturing ($25 million or P1.57 billion) and 1% for digital connectivity ($199 million or P12.50 billion).

“The dealbook only confirms what many suspected, that the Luzon Economic Corridor is, for now, an infrastructure program with a manufacturing label attached to it,” Punongbayan told Rappler on Tuesday, September 15.
That’s not to say we don’t need those railways, ports, pipelines, and power projects. In fact, the Philippines may need to build the boring stuff first before the glamorous industries arrive.

“We need to build the basics first,” Punongbayan said. “Manufacturers tend to go where power, water, and logistics are cheap and reliable, and the corridor’s rail, port, and energy projects could help on that front.”

Independent research analyst and strategic adviser Cesar Tolentino, who worked with Rappler in the previous story to assess how far the LEC projects had progressed, likewise expected more concrete digital infrastructure in the pipeline.

“A communication backbone, especially for New Clark City, is crucial for any infrastructure ecosystem,” Tolentino said. “Locators will be asking for the communication infrastructure before they decide to locate in New Clark City.”
Beyond this, the Philippines has to make itself a more attractive place to do business, especially for investors weighing it against other destinations across the region.
“We have to show ease of doing business and predictability in doing business,” Go told Rappler. “This will need a whole of country collective effort.”

blocks.caption: World Bank sees promise in Pax Silica. Can PH build more than another assembly hub?

blocks.text: The problem is not necessarily a lack of good rules. The World Bank’s latest Business Ready assessment found that Philippine business regulations scored 71 out of 100, nearly matching Singapore’s 72. The difference lay in whether those rules actually worked on the ground.
“Converting good rules into delivery is the next test. Regulation on paper nearly matches Singapore; delivery trails it,” the World Bank said in its report.

The Philippines scored only 53 for the public services needed to implement those regulations, against Singapore’s 70, and 67 for operational efficiency, far behind Singapore’s 87. The difference can translate into weeks of waiting for a company trying to enter the country.

“Currently, it takes 76 days for a foreign firm to be registered in the Philippines. In Singapore, it takes one,” World Bank lead economist Gonzalo Varela said on August 3. “So, working on that agenda, make it easier for firms. You’re going to get more, better firms.”

Hovering over the government’s ambitions is Pax Silica, the US-led initiative that could turn New Clark City into a hub for AI, semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, and critical mineral supply chains.
It’s also a case study of just how difficult that transformation could be.

Pax Silica is closely tied to the Luzon Economic Corridor, with its planned hub in New Clark City meant to deliver precisely the high-tech investments that officials hope the corridor will eventually attract. But it remains very much work in progress.

Pax Silica does not appear among the detailed projects in the current LEC dealbook. No final agreement has been signed and the proposed 2027 national budget contains no allocation for it. Even before the project has fully taken shape, however, it is already being hounded by questions over power, water, environmental costs, and who ultimately stands to benefit.

At full development, Pax Silica could require as much as 3,000 megawatts of electricity, roughly 19% of Luzon’s projected 2026 peak demand. That immediately runs into one of the Philippine manufacturing sector’s oldest weaknesses, with electricity still expensive and reliable supply essential for factories and data centers that cannot afford interruptions.

No less than Energy Secretary Sharon Garin has warned against simply plugging the full load of a built-out Pax Silica into the Luzon grid, calling that prospect “too dangerous for our usual consumers.” Once the project grows large enough, she said, it would likely need a large stand-alone power system rather than risk destabilizing supply for households and other businesses.

And the challenge isn’t merely finding enough megawatts. The Philippines also has to make electricity cheap enough to remain competitive with other countries chasing the same investments. (READ:[READOUT] The race to deliver cheaper power)

“On the single most important constraint for manufacturing in the Philippines, which is the price of electricity, the dealbook is silent,” Punongbayan said. “Beyond tax incentives, what does the government actually have on the table to bring advanced manufacturing here?”

blocks.caption: Building a ‘Silicon Valley in Tarlac’? Manny Pangilinan wants in.

blocks.text: In the end, all of these calculations may have to be reconsidered if Filipinos themselves reject the project.

That opposition was difficult to miss during the very forum where Marcos and foreign officials were selling the corridor’s future. Outside the Grand Hyatt hotel, protesters led by Bayan rallied against Pax Silica, raising concerns over its impact on communities, the environment, and Philippine resources. Demonstrators clashed with police as they tried to reach the hotel lobby.
Human rights group Karapatan said 27 people were injured and five paralegals were arrested.
Inside, investors were being asked to help build the Philippines’ technological future. Outside, protesters were demanding that one of its most ambitious pieces be scrapped. – Rappler.com
*$1 = P62.829 based on the September 14, 2026 rate of the Bankers Association of the Philippines.

articles.title: How climate change worsened Nepal's deadly mountain collapse
articles.summary: A glacier and rock collapse in Nepal killed nearly 1,400 people and left thousands missing. Scientists say decades of warming helped set the disaster in motion.

image.caption: A drone view of flood damage along the Trishuli River in Nuwakot district, Nepal.Image: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nearly 1,400 people have died after a mountain slope collapsed and flash floods swept through the valleys of Nepal and Tibet. More than 5,000 people remain missing.

The collapse was initially thought to have been caused by an earthquake. Now, glaciologists and climate scientists have determined that a complex series of factors led to the disaster, with climate change laying the groundwork several times over: Warming temperatures receded the glacier, thawed permafrost and increased meltwater, destabilizing the slope until it gave way on August 26.

"This was not a single trigger event," Walter Immerzeel, a mountain hydrologist at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, told journalists on a press call. "The failure occurred at an elevation of about 5150 meters (about 16,896 feet) and there were several processes acting together over time scales of years to decades, rather than one factor acting alone."

blocks.caption: With no time to prepare, families in Devighat returned to mud-filled homes days later to salvage whatever survivedImage: Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: How the disaster unfolded

The floods began upstream with a large rock avalanche on the north face of Langtang Lirung. That caused a section of the glacier to collapse at the same time, sending roughly 110 million cubic meters of rock and glacier ice, the size of 44,000 Olympic swimming pools, hurtling downward. That type of rock avalanche is rare, occurring at this size only once every 1,000-10,000 years.

The material fell about 1,400 meters (4,593 feet) from the mountain to the valley floor, picking up debris, water, ice, rock and sediment as it descended. The impact released as much energy as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake. As it crashed into the valley, it also tore up buried glacier ice, adding up to 30 million more cubic meters of debris and water to the flow.

Within about seven minutes, the flood reached Nepal and China's Rasuwagadhi border, 20 kilometers (about 12 miles) downstream, moving at an average speed of 170 kilometers per hour (about 106 miles per hour). The flood continued downstream, traveling 200 kilometers in under seven hours.

blocks.caption: Relatives are going through photographs of missing people, trying to find loved onesImage: Safal Prakash Shrestha/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: How did this happen?

It was a complex combination of conditions, exacerbated by climate change, that allowed the slope to collapse in the first place. That's according to researchers with World Weather Attribution, an international collaboration of scientists that looks at the role of climate change in extreme weather and disaster events.
Rising temperatures, due to the burning of fossil fuels, have reshaped this stretch of the Himalayas for decades.

Near the failure site, the glacier's edge had retreated just 75 meters between 1964 and 2000. But between 2010 and 2026, it dramatically accelerated, retreating another 373 meters. That stripped away the ice supporting the rock wall above it.

Permafrost — or permanently frozen ground within the rock — had also started to thaw. That took place between 4,500 and 5,500 meters of elevation, a critical band that's most sensitive to warming. As it thawed, the mountain walls became more and more unstable.

In the immediate run-up to the collapse, conditions were extreme. July and August overall were the warmest on record in the area, with climate change adding about 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to the region. On August 24 and 25, temperatures ran roughly 2.5 to 2.7 degrees Celsius above the 10-year average. A day before the catastrophe unfolded, the maximum temperature was approximately 7 degrees Celsius above the reference mean.
An unusually snowy October in 2025 likely also played a role, generating more meltwater.

Researchers also believe a 2015 earthquake played a role. That magnitude-7.8 quake triggered an earlier avalanche at Langtang Lirung, which may have weakened the rock mass in the years since, priming the slope for failure.
A disaster beyond adaptation

Researchers also tried to find out whether this was a disaster the region could have prepared for and adapted to. They determined it was uniquely hard to detect, as Nepal's early warning systems are designed for forecastable rainfall-driven floods, not quickly developing, cascading events like this one.
Essentially, this kind of complex threat exceeds the limits of adaptation.

The flood outran Nepal's early warning systems and destroyed several monitoring gauges in its wake. The first mass SMS warning was sent about 38 minutes after the initial collapse, but the flood had already reached the border 7 minutes in.

"When warming destabilizes the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction," Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said.
"Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come."

articles.title: Climate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study finds
articles.summary:
Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August

Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic…

blocks.text: Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.

Researchers identified unusually warm conditions before the glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3,885 cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale, hitting communities downstream without warning.

“Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor at Imperial College London, which carried out the study.

“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”

blocks.caption: A impromptu memorial in Kathmandu commemorates some of the people killed in the flooding. Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPA

blocks.text: More than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.

It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.
The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.

“Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.”

The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.
Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.

Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse.

blocks.caption: ‘Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,’ said Dr Friederike Otto. Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAP

blocks.text: Among the study’s key findings were:
after newsletter promotion

items: In the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically;
July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse;
The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost;
The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater;
A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015 further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed.

blocks.text: Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology.
Clarke said: “We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse.”

blocks.caption: A major earthquake in Nepal in 2015 may also have contributed to the glacier’s collapse. Photograph: Ishwar Rauniyar/The Guardian

blocks.text: Nepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for the disaster.

Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the “losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities”.

He added: “In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that’s done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed.”

articles.title: US Congress passes Russia sanctions bill
articles.summary: The sanctions package is considered the most substantial US legislative effort against Moscow since Trump returned to the White House. It awaits the president's signature, and he has said he will…

image.caption: The bill was passed by 262-159, after breezing through the Senate last month in an 86-11 vote [FILE: Feb 5, 2019]Image: Alex Edelman/CNP/picture alliance

blocks.text: The US Republican-led House of Representatives passed on Wednesday a package of broad new sanctions against Russia over its war in Ukraine.
The bill passed 262-159, after breezing through the Senate in an 86-11 vote last month.
The bill, considered the toughest legislative effort against Russia during US President Donald Trump's second term, awaits the president's signature to come into law. Trump has said he will sign it.
What does the sanctions package against Russia entail?

The package targets Russia's energy and defense sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials. It also targets Moscow's so-called shadow fleet, old tankers it uses to circumvent sanctions.

More controversially, the legislation allows Trump to impose secondary sanctions on countries which rely on Russian oil and gas, in the form of tariffs. China and India are expected to be the main targets of such measures.
The bill would also extend sanctions on Iran.
It was drafted by late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly in July, since April 2025.
But Trump has delayed it, as his foreign policy favors retaining control over tariffs and sanctions rather than leaving such decisions to Congress.

articles.title: IMF downgrades Australian economic forecast amid fears of interest rate hike
articles.summary:
Global financial institution predicts Australia’s GDP will grow to just 1.6% in 2027 as Treasury faces rising energy costs and inflation

  • Get our

blocks.text: The International Monetary Fund has downgraded its forecast for Australia’s economic growth in 2027, warning that the Reserve Bank may have to hike interest rates further to get price pressures back under control.

The IMF also called on federal and state governments to tighten their belts, with a new report saying more disciplined budgets will rein in rising debt burdens and help solve Australia’s long-running inflation problem.

In a “concluding statement” that followed annual consultations with Treasury, RBA and Australian Prudential Regulation Authority officials, the Washington-based institution predicted that the economy would grow by 1.9% this year.
But it shaved 0.1 percentage points off its forecast for real GDP growth to just 1.6% in 2027, flagging the downgrade was due to the higher likelihood of another RBA interest rate hike.
“Inflation remains a central challenge, while weak productivity growth is weighing on the economy’s potential,” the statement said.
“There is a risk that further large increases in global energy prices lead to stronger second-round effects and lift inflation expectations, warranting further tightening” in monetary policy.
The new assessment will come as a blow to Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, who is already under pressure to present a convincing story of improving living standards and prosperity.

Fuel prices in Australia are rising again after the worsening Middle East conflict pushed the global oil benchmark, Brent crude, above US$108 a barrel on Wednesday, marking a 35% surge since the start of August.
As global energy costs climb and threaten to spill over into domestic inflation, financial markets are pricing in an 80% chance of a RBA rate hike on 29 September.
The IMF largely backed – or at least did not overtly criticise – Labor’s budget changes to investor taxes, although it noted widely publicised concerns around unintended consequences.

“Changes to capital gains taxation and negative gearing can reduce housing-related distortions, but continued efforts to minimise compliance costs and impact on investment are needed during implementation,” the report said.
after newsletter promotion
House price falls had done little to address unaffordable housing, the IMF said. It welcomed the steps taken to boost housing supply, even as it urged states and the federal government to do more.

The report noted that the combined federal and state deficit had widened over the past two years as states spent big on infrastructure projects, along with higher social services costs, especially in healthcare and the national disability insurance scheme.
There was also taxpayer money committed to cushioning the impact of the initial global energy price shock, most notably through cuts to the fuel excise.
New South Wales and Queensland spend more than twice as much on debt interest now than before the pandemic, according to Challenger.

And while “Australia’s overall public debt remains relatively low compared to many other advanced economies”, the IMF officials pointed to rising debts and interest costs, especially in state governments.
“The ongoing efforts to restrain general government spending, amidst strong private demand, would also support disinflation efforts by the RBA.”
In the longer term, poor productivity growth was “Australia’s key structural challenge”, the IMF said.
“Reversing the slowdown in recent years will be crucial to improving living standards” and making our public and private debt obligations sustainable over the long run.
The comments come before Monday’s release of the government’s latest intergenerational report, which will paint a long-term and likely challenging picture of Australia’s economy and budget.

articles.title: [Pastilan] The curious case of Sara Duterte’s memory hole
articles.summary: Sara Duterte tries to sweep under the carpet the corruption and anomalies that took place during her father's presidency, while blaming Ferdinand Marcos Jr. as though he and he alone were responsible…

items: Sara Duterte's recent statements downplay the long-standing infrastructure failures and corruption in the Philippines, which have persisted through multiple administrations, including her father's.

The article criticizes Sara for her silence on corruption during her father's presidency and her attempts to shift blame solely onto Ferdinand Marcos Jr., ignoring the collective responsibility of past leaders.
It calls for accountability across all political families and emphasizes the need for citizens to demand answers regarding the misuse of public funds and the integrity of political figures.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Somebody should tell Sara Duterte that people are swimming in floodwaters because her father Rodrigo and other presidents, Ferdinand Marcos Jr. included, failed to do enough to address this country’s chronic infrastructure failures and the corruption that has accompanied them for decades.

Her deliberate omissions as she addressed her supporters outside the court after her arraignment was reset were an insult to the intelligence of Filipinos, as she sought to pretend that this catastrophe began recently, or that it conveniently arrived with the administration she once supported and loved, but now wishes to blame.

The responsibility is collective, and her father had six years in Malacañang in which to confront these problems. He did not solve them. He contributed substantially to them. Decades of incompetent infrastructure planning, grotesque failures of execution, and allegations of corruption have left the country exactly where it is today.

And where was Sara while construction firms associated with then-presidential caregiver and now Senator Bong Go were reportedly collecting government contracts left, right, and center? Some of those contracts involved flood control and other public works. Where was the outrage then?

blocks.caption: Firm owned by Bong Go’s kin once worked with Discayas for Davao projects

blocks.text: Where was Sara when the construction businesses of Sarah and Curlee Discaya, by their own admission, saw their government contracts balloon in 2016, when they expanded their attention from local governments to the Department of Public Works and Highways? That was the year her father began his presidency and placed extraordinary trust in figures such as Chinese ring leader Michael Yang a.k.a. Yang Hongming whom Duterte turned into an economic adviser.

The Duterte years also saw the extraordinary expansion of the Yang syndicate’s Philippine offshore gaming operations and a proliferation of criminal allegations and scandals surrounding parts of that ecosystem, including allegations involving smuggling, illegal drugs, etc.. These are not minor footnotes to history. They are part of the political inheritance that Sara Duterte now seems remarkably eager to edit.

Then came Yang and Pharmally. Billions of pesos in government contracts for COVID-19 pandemic supplies became the subject of investigations and allegations of anomalous procurement, excessive pricing, and substandard and questionable supplies. Filipinos were frightened, dying, unemployed, and confined to their homes while public money was being spent over deals that raised serious questions about who benefited from the national emergency. Sara was not exactly famous for making herself hoarse in protest.

And what did Sara say when her father himself publicly suggested that eliminating corruption was effectively impossible within the existing constitutional framework and floated the idea that the country might need “another Marcos” (dictator) to end it?

Silence. Sara Duterte did not call her father inutile and bangag (slow-minded) – by his own admission, he was using Fentanyl. Instead, she has been trying to sweep all the corruption and anomalies that took place from 2016 to mid-2022 under the carpet.

Now the ambitious Sara wants Filipinos to believe that Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is all to blame – he and he alone – for the country’s institutional rot. This is political amnesia if not intellectual dishonesty. Marcos did not invent decades of failed flood control, inadequate drainage, dysfunctional planning, or corruption. This may have been taking place since his father’s presidency or even much earlier. Nor did he inherit a blank sheet of paper in 2022. But neither does that absolve him of responsibility for what happened under his administration.

The adult position is to hold every administration accountable for its own failures, not to turn politics into a children’s game in which one family is permanently innocent and another is permanently guilty.

Sara’s propaganda is therefore not merely partisan. It is intellectually lazy. It asks Filipinos to forget everything that happened before 2022 and to treat the Duterte administration as though it had not been six years of terribly bad governance.
And now she wants Filipinos to believe that she is the greatest agent of change.
Really?

This is the same politician who could not even say Pax Silica right and then became the subject of ridicule for calling it something resembling “Fox sili.” If the phrase was unfamiliar, that is hardly a crime. But when someone presents herself as uniquely qualified to understand the future while displaying conspicuous unfamiliarity with a major geopolitical and economic initiative, Filipinos are entitled to ask whether the confidence is supported by competence.
“Fox sili” ka diha.
More seriously, why should taxpayers be expected to place unquestioning faith in Sara whose own offices have faced serious questions about the use of confidential funds?
The Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd), during Sara Duterte’s tenure as education secretary, are being scrutinized over their confidential fund expenditures.
The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) was asked to verify thousands of names appearing in the documents associated with those expenditures.

Information from PSA Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande, presented before the Senate impeachment court, showed that of the 2,669 names submitted for verification, 1,685 had no corresponding birth, marriage, or death records. These are based on the PSA database.

The verification reportedly found 37 names corresponding to individuals with death records and 25 corresponding to minors, including infants. One listed individual was reportedly only two months old and had died in 1965.
Two months old. 1965. Let that sink in.
The OVP accounted for 1,992 of the names, of which 1,287 reportedly had no corresponding civil registry records.
The DepEd list contained 677 names, including 398 without matching records.
Those figures constitute precisely the kind of matter that should make any responsible citizen demand answers before handing even more public money to the people responsible.
So before Sara Duterte asks Filipinos to believe that she alone possesses the courage, competence, and moral authority to rescue the country, perhaps she should answer a simpler question.
Where was that courage when her own political house was being built?

And now we hear that a company linked to Sara secured over P15 million in food and catering contracts from the Davao City government and PhilHealth between 2022 and 2025, with its contracts peaking in the very year she became vice president.
Isn’t that an awkward coincidence for anyone preaching about corruption while demanding that Filipinos forget the record of her own political camp?

blocks.caption: Sara Duterte’s company won millions’ worth of contracts from Davao City Hall

blocks.text: More awkward still are questions over her disclosed financial interest in the company and discrepancies between her Statements of Assets Liabilities and Net worth (SALN) and corporate records, because the fight against corruption is rather less convincing when the questions start knocking on your own door.

The country does not need another politician who discovers corruption only when it belongs to an opponent. It does not need another dynasty asking the public to forget the dynasty’s own record. It certainly does not need another presidential campaign disguised as righteous anger.
What the country needs is accountability that does not change according to surname.
That standard has to apply to Marcos, and it has to apply to the Dutertes.
In fact, it has to apply to everyone who has occupied Malacañang, everyone who has controlled a government agency, and everyone who has benefited from the machinery of the state.
The floodwaters do not care which political family is making the speech. Neither should the Filipino voter.
Saba diha, Sara! Pastilan. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sweden's center-left bloc set to win election, STV reports
articles.summary: The center-left opposition won the Swedish elections by a very slim margin, the public broadcaster reported after 99% of the votes were counted. Thorny negotiations await the bloc even if the result…

image.caption: The leading bloc is led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats, the party that ruled Sweden for most of the 20th centuryImage: Jonas Ekströmer/TT News Agency/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sweden's center-left opposition bloc looks set to win the most votes in the country's parliamentary election, albeit by the slimmest of margins, public broadcaster SVT said on Wednesday with 99% of the votes counted.
As of 1647 GMT, with fewer than 1% of votes left to count, the center-left bloc was ahead by just 26,169 votes.
The bloc is led by Magdalena Andersson of the Social Democrats, the party that ruled Sweden for most of the 20th century.
If the results are confirmed, it would usher in a change in government from the right-wing bloc led by Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.

blocks.caption: The election authority was now counting late incoming ballots, such as those from voters abroadImage: Christine Olsson/TT News Agency/REUTERS

blocks.text: What do we know about the Swedish election results so far?

Data from Sweden's election authority shows Kristersson's bloc was on track to win 174 seats, against 175 seats for the center-left. Both Kristersson and Andersson have said they would be open to exploring coalition options.
"The likelihood of a turnaround at this stage is so low that we ​can confidently state that the opposition will secure the most seats in this election," ⁠SVT ​said.
The election authority was counting late incoming ballots from home and overseas, a process expected to continue until Thursday.
Sweden awaits final outcome of razor's-edge election

Even with Andersson's slim lead, her bloc is bracing for tough negotiations before forming any government, especially amid deep divisions between the liberal Center Party and the socialist Left Party.
After the 2022 elections, it took 37 days to form a government, which was considerably shorter than in 2018, when the process took 134 days.
Parliament cannot vote in a new prime minister before September 29.

articles.title: Two teenage boys charged with murder after alleged mistaken identity shooting death of Sydney student
articles.summary: Boys aged 14 and 16 charged after Marco Tapia, 23, was killed inside his family’s home in Glen Alpine

blocks.text: Two teenage boys have been charged with murder after the shooting death of a university student in Sydney this month, which police say was a case of mistaken identity.
Marco Tapia, 23, was shot inside his family’s home in Glen Alpine early on 1 September.
Officers were called to the house just before 4am that day by reports of a home invasion. They found Tapia with a gunshot wound; he died at the scene.

Detectives conducted an extensive investigation, determining that the wrong house had been targeted. Two boys, aged 14 and 16, were arrested on Wednesday and charged with murder. They are not alleged to have shot the weapon.
Both face charges of participating in a criminal group contributing to criminal activity, possession of an unauthorised firearm and driving conveyances taken without the owners’ consent.
The 14-year-old was also charged with damaging property with fire or an explosion.
Police will allege in court that the pair staged vehicles and provided a weapon for the gunman. They have been refused bail and will appear in children’s court on Thursday.
Tapia’s parents spoke to Channel Nine’s A Current Affair this week, saying: “Hate came to our house.” Both were home at the time, as was their daughter.
“I remember him taking the last breath,” his mother, Claudia, told the program.
His father, Sergio, said: “He was a beautiful young man. It’s already impacted a lot of hearts to see such a beautiful person, such a caring, loving man pass in this awful manner.
after newsletter promotion
“It was wasteful, it was useless, it was ridiculously stupid to take such a beautiful person away from this earth.”
The New South Wales police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, has vowed to target those behind a spate of Sydney shootings. Another man was killed on 2 September.
“One innocent victim is unacceptable to me,” he told reporters after Tapia’s death. “We won’t rest until we stop this violence … anything we can do to stop it, we will do.”

articles.title: US lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablers
articles.summary:
Act divides Democrats and Republicans, with some saying it gives president power that could be turned against US allies

The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Donald Trump to…

blocks.text: The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Donald Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power.

The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago.

The long delay in the vote was widely considered to be scepticism from the Trump administration, which had opposed additional sanctions and then recently changed its stance to support tabling the bill as efforts to negotiate with the Kremlin to end the war have yielded few results.

However the bill faced last-minute hurdles in Congress as members of the Republican party’s isolationist wing were joined by Democrats who warned that Trump could use the bill’s new tariffs authority against allies instead.

The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports.
It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions.

Senior Democrats voiced opposition to the bill during a heated floor debate. “Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” said Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the House, during a speech on Wednesday, adding he would vote against the bill.

Democratic staffers supporting the bill said that it offered a “last chance” to increase sanctions on Russia before Ukraine entered a “long winter”. Russia has improved the drone technology it has used to strike Ukrainian infrastructure as Kyiv has suffered a shortage of anti-air missiles, leaving the country in a dire position.
Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican supporting the bill, called it the US Congress’ “Churchill vs Chamberlain Moment on Russia”.

“Choking off the money funding a war of conquest in Europe is exactly what that authority should be used for, and Congress deciding to do that is Congress doing its constitutional job,” he said, rejecting arguments by Democrats that the bill gave Trump too much authority to slap tariffs on foreign countries.

The bill passed the Senate last month in a landslide 86-11 vote. However it faced more pushback in the House of Representatives. A Tuesday rule vote allowing consideration of Senate amendments to the bill passed by just 214-211, with two renegade Democrats joining Republicans to vote in favour of what they said was an act of support for Ukraine. That vote led to senior Democrats holding terse talks with their fellow party members.

“I’m proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America – people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism,” wrote Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the two Democrat representatives, in a statement on Tuesday.

“I’ll always stand with my community’s values, and am grateful for the 86 senators who voted to send this bill to the House. My vote today gets us one step closer to enacting these sanctions into law and I look forward to voting tomorrow to cut off the flow of Russian oil money fuelling this war.”

The Ukrainian government has said it supported the bill, and hundreds of pro-Ukrainian activists calling for tougher sanctions on Russia held advocacy talks in Washington DC in the days leading up to the vote.

“We support any initiative that is in the interest of Ukraine and Ukrainians,” said Denys Sienik, the Chargé d’Affaires at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington DC. “So if we are talking about the possibility of putting more pressure on Russia so that it holds the Russian war machine, of course, we are there, and we are grateful to every senator, to every congressman and congresswoman for their voice and, and for their support.”

articles.title: Canada wants into Britain's rapid-response defence club
articles.summary: Canada has formally applied to join the United Kingdom's Joint Expeditionary Force, reversing a decision made more than a decade ago. Born from the Afghanistan war and reshaped by Russia's invasion…

image.caption: Canadian Armed Forces members are seen participating in drills in Cambridge Bay, Nunavut, in February. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Canada has formally applied to join the United Kingdom's Joint Expeditionary Force, reversing a decision made more than a decade ago. Born from the Afghanistan war and reshaped by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the coalition promises speed and flexibility — but raises an old question about what Canada is actually committing itself to.
Formal application to Joint Expeditionary Force announced during Carney's U.K. visit
Canada has formally applied to join the U.K.-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a collection of NATO nations whose mandate is to respond more quickly in a crisis.
Prime Minister Mark Carney formally announced the plan on Wednesday while meeting with his British counterpart Andy Burnham.

In a statement, Carney called JEF an "important initiative" and highlighted other close defence ties with the U.K., including Canada's observer status in the development of the next generation of fighter jet.

Canada was asked by the U.K. more than dozen years ago to join JEF after it was formed in the waning days of the war in Afghanistan. The concept was discussed at the 2014 NATO leaders' summit in Wales, but ultimately the government of former prime minister Stephen Harper rebuffed the overtures.

items: Canada joining international program to build next generation of fighter jets
Canada urges U.K. to join new global bank for defence projects

blocks.text: The Canadian military, at the time in the throes of deep budget cuts by Conservative government of the day, was also deeply reluctant to join.

In an interview with The Canadian Press at the time, the commander of the military's joint operations command, Lt.-Gen. Jonathan Vance, who later became the chief of the defence staff, said there were a number of concerns about joining the British expeditionary force.

It would be, he said, a substantial undertaking for the military and could bind the country to respond in a specific way to a future crisis when the federal government might favour a different course.
Joining the force without a specific mission, Vance said in 2014, would signal "a commitment to future operations, having done the training, that you may — or may not — be able to honour."

In his statement on Wednesday, Carney did not say how Canada's participation in JEF would work on a practical level. And the country's current top military commander, Gen. Jennie Carignan, has yet to weigh in on what the membership might mean.
As it was originally conceived, the Joint Expeditionary Force was meant to preserve battlefield relationships that grew up during the Afghan war.

In 2012, Britain's then chief of defence staff, Gen. Sir David Richards, described a future force that could deploy rapidly overseas without Britain having to assemble an entirely new coalition for every crisis.
It was thought at the time that the British Army would provide the command structure and much of the military backbone and other countries would bring forces that plug into JEF as needed.
Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 gave the idea urgency.

At the NATO summit in Wales that year, Britain, Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands and Norway formally agreed to establish JEF under NATO's new Framework Nations Concept. Finland and Sweden joined in 2017, before either country belonged to NATO, and Iceland entered the fold in 2021.
There is an important distinction to make. While JEF is made up of NATO nations, the organization has no equivalent of NATO's Article 5 collective defence clause.

items: First phase of Army restructuring creates division focused on defending Canada
Canada, Ukraine forge 100-year pact built on drones and defence
No longer taboo, Canada's defence industry steps into Europe's spotlight

blocks.text: It is essentially a coalition of willing states that can assemble forces for a particular contingency without requiring consensus among all NATO members.
There have been a series of military exercises held under the JEF banner since 2018.
But Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 turned JEF from an expeditionary military concept into something approaching a Northern European security coalition.

A 2024 research report by the U.K.-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) argued that JEF had genuine advantages, notably speed of decision-making compared with NATO, but it has not been seriously tested politically or operationally.
The study said that the expeditionary force is not actually a standing military body and governments provide forces when required.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

articles.title: US government paid federal employees $9.5bn not to work amid Doge cuts – report
articles.summary:
GAO report shows how use paid administrative leave rose by 435% from 2023 to 2025 and incurred a sixfold cost

The US government paid federal workers $9.5bn not to work in 2025 as part of the…

blocks.text: The US government paid federal workers $9.5bn not to work in 2025 as part of the Trump administration’s attempts to shrink the federal workforce.

As part of efforts by the “department of government efficiency” (Doge), spearheaded by Elon Musk, federal agencies’ use of paid administrative leave rose 435% from 2023 to 2025 – costing six times what the government spent in 2023 – according to a new report released on Tuesday by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), an independent watchdog.
Of the $9.5bn paid to federal workers, $6.7bn was associated with the deferred resignation program.

“Paid administrative leave for federal employees is an excused absence without loss of pay or charge to leave. It is a cost to taxpayers as employees receive full pay without performing job duties,” the GAO said.

It added: “The number of workdays of paid administrative leave reported increased from about 4m workdays and 4.4m workdays in calendar years 2023 and 2024, respectively, to about 21.6m workdays in 2025.”

About 70% of the paid administrative leave used in 2025 was tied to the deferred resignation program, according to the GAO. Across the 76 agencies reviewed, 144,312 employees reported taking paid administrative leave under the program.

Since January 2023, the Trump administration has reduced the federal US workforce by approximately 355,000 employees, leaving many struggling to find new jobs while others have been rehired after the administration determined that too many positions had been eliminated.
Speaking to the Guardian, Douglas Pasternak, research director of Public Citizen’s Trump Accountability Project, described the federal overhaul efforts as “haphazard”.

“There are multiple examples of how this was not thought out,” Pasternak said, adding: “It’s very clear that the Trump administration gave zero forethought to these cuts and to these deferred resignation programs. They haphazardly went out and cut federal workers, and now we’re dealing with the ripple effects of that.”

He pointed to delays in social security check deliveries, longer wait times at Veterans Affairs hospitals for patients seeking critical medical and mental health care, and cuts to federal firefighters. Pasternak also cited reductions at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which has since sought to rehire personnel.
after newsletter promotion

“It’s a case study in mismanagement in how people went about this and it impacted everyone of all political stripes … To simply say we’re going to have fewer workers and therefore less costs is not the way to look at this. You need to look at it in a more sophisticated way, like what do those workers actually do? How do they improve the government? How do they actually help … provide critical resources for the American public?” Pasternak said.

In response to the GAO report, Patty Murray, vice-chair of the Senate appropriations committee, released a statement condemning the federal layoffs, saying: “After promising to cut waste, Trump instead set billions upon billions in taxpayer dollars on fire to quite literally pay people not to do jobs they loved – from researching cancer cures to taking care of our national parks, and so much else.
“Trump spent billions to push out experienced and badly needed experts across government – this was the most expensive way imaginable to make government worse,” Murray added.

articles.title: Exiled Nicaraguan journalist Luis Galeano detained by ICE in Florida
articles.summary:
Galeano, who has had asylum application pending for about seven years, was pulled over by agents while driving for Lyft

Veteran journalist Luis Galeano, one of at least

blocks.text: Veteran journalist Luis Galeano, one of at least 94 Nicaraguans whom the Ortega Murillo regime has stripped of citizenship in recent years for opposing the government, has been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Galeano, who has continued critically reporting on the Sandinista government online through his platform, Café con voz, since shortly after arriving in the US in 2018, has had an asylum application pending for about seven years, according to his wife, Daykel Santamaría. He also has a work permit and a social security number, she said.

Nonetheless, shortly after beginning his second job driving Lyft on Monday morning in Florida, ICE agents pulled him over. As of Wednesday, Galeano was detained at Krome detention center in Miami. He has an immigration court date scheduled for 2 October, Santamaría said.

“Deporting [Galeano] to Nicaragua would be a death sentence,” said Javier Melendez, a sociologist who has been friends with the journalist for more than 30 years. The Sandinista government also stripped Melendez of his citizenship; he’s now a US citizen, living in Washington DC. The denaturalization order also affected acclaimed novelist Sergio Ramírez and poet and writer Gioconda Belli.
Ice has been contacted for comment.

Melendez called the situation facing his friend “a double trauma – he escaped from his country because of his work and then the place where he sought refuge detains him due to their domestic politics”.

Galeano fled Nicaragua in December, 2018, days after police raided 100% Noticias, the outlet where he worked, and issued an order for his arrest. He arrived in Miami shortly thereafter and petitioned for asylum, according to Santamaría.
Santamaría said she didn’t know if her husband was, effectively, a man without a country due to the 2023 measure denaturalizing him as a Nicaraguan.

Meanwhile, on Tuesday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee had a two hour-plus hearing on “Confronting the Totalitarian Ortega-Murillo Regime.” Florida Rep. María Elvira Salazar, committee chairperson, opened the hearing by denouncing how Daniel Ortega and Rosa Murillo “have spent years dismantling democracy”, and warned that “the Administration is paying attention, and Ortega and Murillo should consider themselves warned.”

The disjunction between the US government locking up a journalist targeted by the Nicaraguan government for reporting on its totalitarian tendencies, while at the same time denouncing those same tendencies is an example of “the serious and profound contradictions” in the Trump administration when it comes to Nicaragua, said Ana María Méndez Dardón, Central America director at the Washington Office on Latin America.
Galeano’s detention is one example many of “how due process is missing from the right to asylum” under the Trump administration, she added.

Salazar issued a statement after Galeano’s detention saying: “America must always know the difference between a criminal and a political exile.” Queries from the Guardian to the committee and several of its members were not answered.

Galeano’s detention has also been denounced by Salazar’s GOP colleague in Florida, Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart, who posted a statement on X saying, “The United States has long been a beacon of freedom for those persecuted by tyranny. We must uphold that tradition…”
The Committee to Protect Journalists and the Inter American Press Association called for Galeano’s release.

Although Galeano escaped Nicaragua under threat of arrest in late 2018, records of him being targeted for his reporting date at least as far back as 23 Feb., 2011, when Amnesty International issued a bulletin titled, “Urgent Action,” warning that his life was in danger after “an unknown individual called [him] on his mobile phone and said ‘You have 72 hours to change your mind about what you’ll publish, otherwise your family won’t see you anymore.’”
The caller referred to Galeano’s reporting for El Nuevo Diario on government misuse of around $20m between 2004 and 2008.

Recently, the journalist had been seeing ICE agents in the streets of Miami with increasing alarm while driving Lyft. “He called me like a week ago, asking if I could help with a new journalism project he had in mind, a morning news program on the region [of Latin America],” said Melendez, who founded Expediente Abierto, a think tank on Central America.
“He wanted to get off the streets, seeing the raids everywhere,” Melendez said.

Santamaría, Galeano’s wife, said the two had spoken often about what would happen if one or the either was detained. Plans included calling their lawyer, alerting the media, trying to stay calm. “We prepared ourselves mentally for this moment,” she said.
“We’ve already lived through going into exile, having an order of arrest – these are situations that make you more mature,” she said.

Galeano spoke with his wife several times Wednesday. She described him as calm, telling her, “If God got me out of Nicaragua, he’ll get me out of here.” She said she has faith the US government will see what she called “a very well-documented asylum case”.

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney waves as he and his wife Diana Fox Carney arrive to board a government plane in Ottawa earlier this summer. Fox Carney was appointed to two roles around ocean conservation on Wednesday. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics

Diana Fox Carney — Prime Minister Mark Carney's wife — is stepping into an unpaid role focused on ocean conservation, including chairing an international conference set to take place in Halifax next year.
Halifax to host international conference on ocean conservation in 2027
Diana Fox Carney — Prime Minister Mark Carney's wife — is stepping into an unpaid role focused on ocean conservation.

As the country's ocean envoy, Fox Carney will "advance Canada's leadership by connecting ocean conservation, climate action, Indigenous leadership, economic resilience and maritime security," according to a news release.
Fox Carney will also chair the 12th annual Our Ocean Conference, an international gathering that convenes governments, organizations and academics to address modern ocean issues.
The conference will take place in Halifax next year.

"Canada has an opportunity to showcase its leadership in ocean conservation, sustainable fisheries, ocean science and Indigenous-led stewardship" at the 2027 conference, Minister of Fisheries Joanne Thompson said in a statement.
Ocean issues will get global attention in Halifax in 2027
"I look forward to working with Diana Fox Carney on this important conference for Canada."
The announcement said the upcoming conference is an important step toward Ottawa's commitment to protect 30 per cent of Canada's marine and coastal areas by 2030.

"The conference will provide an opportunity to deepen co-operation, share knowledge and experience and secure commitments to ensure healthy and sustainable oceans for future generations," Fox Carney said in a statement.
Career in economics, environment
Until now, Fox Carney's role largely remained on the periphery of her husband's first 18 months as Canada's 24th prime minister.

Having originally drawn Carney's attention by skating circles around her hockey opponents at the University of Oxford — where they were both students and where the now prime minister played goalie on the men's team — Fox Carney has built a notable career as an economist and environmentalist in her own right.
Fox Carney holds master's degrees in agricultural economics from Oxford and international relations from the University of Pennsylvania.

items: Carney announces $3.8B to protect nature, new conservation sites in James Bay and Manitoba
Canada promised new parks and nature protection. Has that shifted with Carney in power?

blocks.text: Throughout her career, Fox Carney has served on the boards of a number of not-for-profit organizations and has held senior roles at prominent think-tanks in both Canada and the U.K., championing environmental issues and income equality among other issues.
In 2013, she drew controversy over a paper she contributed to the Canada 2020 think-tank looking to reignite discussions on carbon pricing in Canada.
Putting a price on carbon
In 2021, Fox Carney started a new role as senior adviser at the Eurasia Group, a political research and consulting firm which offers advice to businesses and politicians around the world.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
David Cummings is a reporter for CBC News.
