articles.title: Key MILF figures fail to make BARMM’s first parliament
articles.summary: COTABATO CITY—Several personalities with long-standing ties to the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) were not among those who will serve in the first regular Bangsamoro Parliament following…

blocks.text: COTABATO CITY—Several personalities with long-standing ties to the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) were not among those who will serve in the first regular Bangsamoro Parliament following Monday’s balloting.

Most of them are incumbent members of the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA), or the interim Bangsamoro Parliament, but did not make it to the regular parliament, whose mandate will begin on Oct. 30 this year and end on June 30, 2031.

The United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP), the MILF’s regional political party, won 15 of the 40 seats allotted to the party list system in the 80-member parliament. Thirty-two seats are for single parliamentary districts, while eight seats are for sectoral representatives.

Abdullah Macapaar, alias “Commander Bravo,” was the No. 22 nominee of the UBJP. He has served as a member of Parliament (MP) since March 29, 2019, as an MILF nominee to the BTA, the interim body tasked with governing the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) during the transition period.
Akmad “Commander Jack” Abas, another longtime field commander of the MILF, also did not make it to the regular parliament, having been the UBJP’s No. 17 nominee.
Narrow loss

Also defeated was professor Hashim Manticayan, the UBJP candidate for the Third Parliamentary District of Cotabato City. He narrowly lost to fellow MILF member Tomanda Antok, who ran under the Bangsamoro Federalist Party (BFP).
Incumbent BTA member Lanang Ali Jr. also failed to secure a seat in the incoming parliament as the UBJP’s No. 19 nominee.
MP Abdullah Hashim, son of MILF founding chair Salamat Hashim, also failed to secure a seat in the regular parliament. He was the UBJP’s No. 21 nominee.
Like Macapaar and Abas, Hashim served in the BTA from 2019 to the present.
MP Bailing Mantawil and former MP Eddie Alih also failed to secure seats, as they were the UBJP’s Nos. 23 and 32 nominees, respectively.
Mantawil concurrently serves as the Bangsamoro minister of science and technology.
MILF Chair Ahod “Al Haj Murad” Ebrahim is the first nominee of the UBJP. He and the 14 other UBJP nominees who will serve in the incoming regular parliament were proclaimed Tuesday night.
Ebrahim stressed that the electoral outcome marked another significant milestone in the Bangsamoro struggle.
“It demonstrated the transformation of decades of sacrifice, perseverance, and steadfast pursuit of self-determination into a democratic mandate for the MILF leadership,” he said.

“The electoral process represents not an end to the struggle, but a new chapter in advancing the aspirations of the Bangsamoro through peaceful, democratic, and principled political engagement,” Ebrahim added.
The BFP, a major party that also includes several MILF members, won 16 of the 40 seats allotted to the party list system.

articles.title: Gordie Howe bridge vehicle traffic tops 340,000 in first full month of operation
articles.summary: Traffic at the new Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit topped 340,000 in its first full month of operation, according to new data.

image.caption: The Gordie Howe International Bridge connects Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, adding a publicly-owned competition to the privately-owned Ambassador Bridge. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor·New
Traffic at the new Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Windsor, Ont., and Detroit topped 340,000 in its first full month of operation, according to new data.
New bridge traffic was nearly on par with nearby Ambassador Bridge
There were 343,507 crossings at the bridge in August, the first full month it was open, per fresh figures from the Bridge and Tunnel Operators Association.
It was nearly the same as traffic at the nearby Ambassador Bridge, which saw 345,445 crossings last month.
But the composition of the traffic on the competing spans was different. The majority of crossings at the Gordie Howe bridge were passenger vehicles: Nearly 270,000 vs. roughly 74,000 trucks.
At the Ambassador, truck traffic was around 150,000, compared to 196,000 passenger cars.

items: Ambassador Bridge 'aggressively' pursued trucking clients amid Gordie Howe delay: industry rep
New bridge, same traffic: Why is the road to the Ambassador Bridge still packed with trucks?

blocks.text: Jason Miller, a supply chain management professor at Michigan State University, says he believes many trucking companies have toll price contracts with the Ambassador Bridge.

"So what's happening is they are probably locked in for this year," he told Windsor Morning on Wednesday. "So it does not make as much sense for them to shift trucks over to Gordie Howe until they would have some type of renegotiated contract or they themselves have a contractual price with Gordie Howe."
LISTEN | Gordie Howe bridge attracts more cars than trucks in first full month of operation:
Windsor Morning6:52Gordie Howe Bridge attracts more cars than trucks in first full month of operation
The Windsor-Detroit Tunnel still had the highest volume of passenger vehicles, with approximately 280,000 crossings in August.
StatsCan data offers different look
Recently released numbers from Statistics Canada offer a more detailed look at the origin of the people crossing the various ports of entry in the Windsor-Detroit corridor.

"In August, the Gordie Howe International Bridge was used for 134,900 Canadian-resident return trips from the United States by automobile, 56.7 per cent of which were same-day," the federal agency said Friday. "It was also used as a port of entry for 101,000 US-resident trips to Canada by automobile, 52.2 per cent of which were same-day.
"During the same period, 348,000 Canadian and US residents entered Canada by automobile at Windsor's Ambassador Bridge and the Windsor-Detroit Tunnel, down 35.4 per cent from August 2025."
The agency also said that 34,800 commercial transport trucks entered Canada using the Gordie Howe Bridge last month.
"Commercial transport truck entries at Windsor's other ports increased by 0.4 per cent from the same period one year earlier to total 87,400," it added.
Miller said traffic volumes at the three crossings are likely to shift in the months ahead as the "novelty effect" of taking the brand new Gordie Howe bridge wears off.
In any case, he said the traffic volumes at the new span being nearly as high as those at the Ambassador Bridge show "the need for that second crossing."

items: Some pedal-assist e-bikes are now allowed on the Gordie Howe Bridge. Here's what this means for cyclists
The CBC's Emma Loop crosses the Gordie Howe International Bridge on foot

blocks.text: "What I'm really curious to see is if there's any information [to] come out about the wait times at either bridge, because that that to me is the most important thing beyond just the crossings, is just that smoother flow of commerce," he added.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Emma Loop is a video journalist at CBC Windsor. She previously spent eight years covering politics, national security, and business in Washington, D.C. Before that, she covered Canadian politics in Ottawa. She has worked at the Windsor Star, Ottawa Citizen, Axios, and BuzzFeed News, where she was a member of the FinCEN Files team that was named a finalist for the 2021 Pulitzer Prize in International Reporting. She was born and raised in Essex County, Ont. You can reach her at emma.loop@cbc.ca.

articles.title: US interest rates raised for first time in three years
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve unanimously voted to increase interest rates to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% on Wednesday.

blocks.text: US interest rates have been raised for the first time in more than three years and could be increased further in a bid to slow rising prices.
Rates were hiked to 3.75%-4% from 3.5%-3.75% by the Federal Reserve in a unanimous decision on Wednesday despite fierce opposition from President Donald Trump, who had called for rates to be cut.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the move was because "inflation is too high and has been for too long", adding that it was a "sober" and "responsible decision".
However, Trump said rates "should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World - BY FAR".
Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for people wanting to secure loans, mortgages and credit cards, but can lead to better returns on savings.
Warsh said while there was "an attitude of optimism" within the Federal Reserve leadership, inflation remained a problem.
"For more than five years, inflation has been running above target," he said. "The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long."
Central banks tend to increase rates when inflation is high to discourage spending and encourage saving in the hope this will reduce the pace of price rises.
But it's a balancing act, as higher rates can also encourage businesses to hold off on investing and hurt economic growth.

Ahead of the mid-term elections in November, affordability is one of the top concerns of American voters, who have seen diesel prices hit an all-time high and petrol rise above $4 (£2.99) a gallon on average.
Global oil prices have surged since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran, driving up the price of car fuel as well as the cost of goods and services generally.

Warsh told a press conference following the decision to raise interest rates that the Fed "cannot affect any individual price whether it be oil prices, whether it be food stuffs at the grocery store", but could ensure price rises do not broaden across the economy.
He added that strong jobs market and wider economy meant the Fed was focused on stablising prices, adding that those least well off had most to gain from lower inflation.

Asked about the message the decision sent to Trump, Warsh chuckled before saying "I have got nothing for you on a discussion with the president," as he batted away similar questions with the same response.
The Federal Reserve is independent of the government, but has faced sharp criticism from Trump over its decisions on rates in recent years.
Trump was heavily critical of Warsh's predecessor Jerome Powell, who stepped down at the end of his term earlier this year, for not cutting rates.
Following Wednesday's announcement, Trump said rates should be cut to "1%, or less".
"LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!", he posted on social media.

Earlier a White House press secretary Kush Desai told Fox News the president and White House had "reiterated our commitment to the independence of the Federal Reserve on numerous occasions" but added it did not prevent Trump being able to voice his opinions.
Warsh said at the press conference that "part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane".
This hike by the Fed is the first move rate move in any direction since they were cut in December 2025. The last time they were raised was in July 2023.
A 0.25pp increase will likely add to increasing mortgage rates for homebuyers, as the rates set by banks and other lenders are heavily influenced by the Fed's policy rate.
Major US banks JP Morgan, KeyCorp and BNY raised their prime lending rate on Wednesday to 7% from 6.75% in response, which will rates charged on credit cards and personal loans.
Mortgage costs have climbed over the past year but remain below peaks seen in 2023. A 30-year fixed deal is 6.76% on average, while a 15-year deal is 6.09%, according to figures from Freddie Mac.

Due to many US homeowners having 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, changes to interest rates will not impact monthly repayments, though they could affect those looking to secure a loan for a home or refinance.

Warsh declined to provide his own view on where he saw interest rates going into the future, but the majority of his fellow policymakers said they believe rates would be hiked again before the end of this year to between 4-4.25%.
A small majority said rates could rise further to the 4.25-4.5% next year, before cuts begin in 2028 and 2029.
The forecast suggested price rises will ease in the coming years, with inflation, the measure used to assess the cost of living, predicted to fall steadily to the Fed's 2% target by 2029.

The US is not alone in tackling the inflation impact from the conflict in the Middle East, with the European Central Bank raising rates last week and the Bank of England set to make its own decision on Thursday.

The memorandum also directs the U.S. trade representative to monitor Canada's treatment of U.S. origin goods in Canadian government procurement.

The latest round of U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods took effect just after midnight Tuesday, adding 50 per cent levies to more than 100 products, including specific cheeses, motorboats, all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) and furniture.
Trump hits Canada with new tariffs and product import bans
The ongoing trade war ramped up in recent weeks after the U.S. and Canada failed to reach a trade agreement in August.

On Aug. 22, the U.S. followed through on a threat of 50 per cent tariffs on a wide swath of Canadian goods. Canada retaliated with its own tariffs on nearly 700 categories of U.S. goods, which came into effect on Sept. 8.

articles.title: Documentary alleges Israel bombs Gaza regardless of risk to civilians
articles.summary: The documentary film NAZA is stirring outrage in Israel, prompting many to defend their military's actions in Gaza against accusations it approves strikes regardless of harm to Palestinian civilians,…

image.caption: Filmmakers Yuval Abraham, left, and Rachel Szor pose with the special jury prize for their documentary NAZA at the Venice International Film Festival on Saturday. The film's allegations about the war in Gaza have angered many Israelis. (Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The documentary film NAZA is stirring outrage in Israel, prompting many to defend their military's actions in Gaza against accusations it approves strikes regardless of harm to Palestinian civilians, while the filmmakers question why critical reflection is being stonewalled.
NAZA got a standing ovation at the Venice festival, but the IDF is exploring legal action
On the streets of Jerusalem, there’s no debating whether the directors of the documentary film NAZA, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, are truth-tellers or traitors.
They should be "in jail for betraying the country, betraying the army, betraying Jewish [people] all over the world,” said Revital Hershko.

Hershko, like many in Israel, has been watching media coverage about the film, which got a special jury prize and a 25-minute standing ovation when it premiered at the Venice International Film Festival last week.

Over roughly an hour and a half, NAZA details Israeli war tactics used in Gaza including AI systems that, by design, target wanted individuals in civilian spaces like apartment buildings — killing average Palestinians.
Abraham and Szor are Israeli, prompting many to label them as lying traitors.

"I think they make a very bad damage to our country. It's not true what they said. They lie. All the soldiers, they didn't do anything," said Dalia Shemtov, a resident of Netanya who was out with friends in Jerusalem when she overheard CBC News asking locals about the film and what they’ve heard.
While many of the people CBC spoke with are furious about the film, no one had seen it, since it’s still only on the festival circuit.
Why the film NAZA is causing uproar in Israel

It’s grabbing headlines because of the people featured — not Palestinians talking about the tens of thousands of people killed in Gaza after nearly three years of Israel's war with Hamas, but because of 24 Israeli military and intelligence personnel.

They describe, albeit anonymously, how attacks are approved and their statements counter official lines coming from the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) that it goes to great lengths to reduce the number of civilian casualties.
The IDF has rejected the film's allegations, saying because only anonymous sources are used there is no way to verify if they have had any direct knowledge of Israeli military operations.

It has also labelled one claim from the trailer as "completely false" — in which a man says he was aware of approval for an airstrike to kill 500 people. Although he does say he does not know exactly how many died because there was no official count.
Lt.-Gen Eyal Zamir, the IDF's chief of general staff, on Monday instructed military lawyers to explore legal options against the filmmakers.
The film was produced by the British newspaper the Guardian, which in a statement said it "will robustly defend" NAZA and its team "from any attacks or attempts at censorship."
Abraham says he and Szor felt a responsibility as Israelis to use their position and abilities to bring insider testimony to light.
"There is a direct correlation between the silence or between the denial of the crimes and their ability to persist,” he said at a news event in Venice.
Fellow Israeli filmmaker Uri Rosenwaks has created an online petition in support of the film, calling on those "still fighting for freedom of expression" to sign.

But the criticisms keep coming. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a video released by his Likud Party, called the film "shocking" and said it's "intolerable" that Israel must "fight antisemitic incitement" both globally and within.
And a man who was held captive in Gaza for 505 days said on Instagram: "I'm angry on a level I can’t describe."

Eliya Cohen was among the 251 people kidnapped in the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, when militants crossed into Israel — killing 1,200 Israelis and foreign workers and igniting Israel's war on Hamas, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in Gaza, according to officials there.

items: Israel committed genocide in Gaza, deliberately targeted Palestinian children: UN report
Remaining supporting acts quit Ed Sheeran tour amid backlash over Macklemore ousting

blocks.text: In his video, translated for CBC News, Cohen says he wants to see pictures of Abraham and Szor posted outside and "across every possible media platform, so that when they walk down the street … they should feel ashamed."
North American audiences will get to reach their own conclusions when NAZA plays at the New York Film Festival, which begins Sept. 25.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Crystal Goomansingh is a correspondent based in London, U.K.

blocks.text: Albanese government to improve safety in child support system

blocks.caption: Tom McIlroy

blocks.text: Tom McIlroy
Tanya Plibersek and Katy Gallagher have announced plans to close gaps that have allowed family and domestic violence perpetrators to continue causing harm through the child support system.

The new rules will scrap legal requirements that any information provided by one parent be shared with the other parent, stopping situations where sharing that information could put children or a parent at risk.

Families will also be supported to recover more unpaid child support debts when they move into official arrangements, and new rules will be created to remove the harm that can arise from family tax benefit debts caused by child support payers against their former partners.
In a joint statement, the social services minister and the finance minister said:

double quotation markThere is almost $2 billion of unpaid child support in this country. There are almost 100,000 parents and carers in the child support system who have experienced or are at risk of experiencing family and domestic violence. Australian children deserve better. This is the first stage of the most significant reforms to child support in decades, helping create a system that is safer, simpler and more effective for Australian families.
Australia breaks into top 10 global gender gap rankings

blocks.caption: Ima Caldwell

blocks.text: Ima Caldwell
Australia has broken into the top 10 of the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Report, ranking eighth out of 148 countries – its highest ranking ever.
The 2026 report marks a significant climb for Australia, moving up 35 places from 43rd since the Albanese government took office.

The government credits this historic high to improved political representation (including a majority-female cabinet), expanded paid parental leave, wage increases in female-dominated sectors and new investments in women’s health.
Anthony Albanese said in a statement that the ranking “slipped to an all-time low of 50th under the previous Coalition government” and acknowledged that the work must continue:

double quotation markThe job is not done and we will continue to focus our efforts on lifting wages, ending gender-based violence, increasing female representation in workplaces, investing in women’s health and more.
The minister for women, Katy Gallagher, said the record ranking was “not by accident”, also recognising areas for improvement:

double quotation markWe know there is more work to do across our priorities of ending violence against women, valuing care, improving women’s economic empowerment, improving women’s health outcomes and strengthening women’s leadership and representation – this is just one measure that shows Australia is moving in the right direction.

blocks.caption: Katy Gallagher. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP

blocks.text: International student visa changes expected
International students will see some of the biggest changes in the reform of immigration settings.

Last year Australia issued more than 337,000 international student visas, of which about 45,000 went to dependents or family members of the primary applicant. The vast majority of students will now be expected to be required to come alone.
Burke gave a preview in parliament yesterday.

double quotation markWe do need to get net overseas migration down. We need to make sure that we deal with the numbers overall, and do so in a sensible, a targeted way that provides the easiest pathway through the Australian economy.
Burke’s speech kicks off at 12.30pm today.
Long-anticipated immigration changes drop today
Foreign students will face tough restrictions on the ability to bring family members into Australia under big changes to the country’s immigration system.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, will reveal the changes today at the National Press Club, after plans for a speech more than a month ago were derailed.
Burke’s plan is designed to bring down net overseas migration (Nom) while doing the least damage to the economy.
His speech is titled: “The work of managing the migration program: Who arrives, who stays, who leaves”.

The plan will shift some rules for visa categories away from demand-driven settings, introduced during the Howard government, allowing more control on the numbers of people coming into, and departing, the country.
Labor plans to use legislation to gain more control over arrival numbers but could rely on regulation and directives to departmental officials if it cannot find agreement in parliament.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it will be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

articles.title: Drake's FOMO film takes fans on a Toronto-filled summer ride, featuring new music and Iron Man suits
articles.summary: Drake fans were treated to a little bit of everything — including several new tracks — when the rapper dropped his much anticipated "not so short film" on Tuesday night.

image.caption: Drake performing at a show at Scotiabank Arena in Toronto on Oct. 26, 2025. The rapper dropped an hour-long 'not so short film' featuring new music on Tuesday. (Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Drake fans were treated to a little bit of everything — including several new tracks — when the rapper dropped his much anticipated "not so short film" on Tuesday night.
Rapper livestreamed hour-long film, featuring 9 new tracks and many guest appearances, on Tuesday
He described it as such when he teased it on Instagram last week — and he wasn't lying.
Clocking in at about an hour and livestreamed to YouTube, Spotify and Apple, Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) took viewers for a ride of Drake's summer escapades and lavish lifestyle.
The film featured Drizzy dancing through his palatial Toronto mansion, kee-keeing with his mom Sandra Graham and her besties, and riding toward the Toronto skyline in his lime-green luxury speedboat.

items: 'It's going to be a Drake summer': Reactions pour in on Iceman's triple-album drop

blocks.text: True to form, the video was peppered with Toronto- and Canada-specific references and Easter eggs, including a scene of Drake striding through the Canadian National Exhibition alongside fellow rapper Loe Shimmy, both decked out in $150,000 Iron Man suits.
The film was packed with star power, featuring guest appearances from SexyyRed, Stunna Sandy, model Winnie Harlow, NBA star Kevin Durant, porn star Lena the Plug and more.

Much like Drake's ICEMAN livestream four months ago — sections of which he repurposed in a visual album for tracks from his HABIBTI and MAID OF HONOUR albums — FOMO promo'd some new music, including unreleased collaborations with Don Toliver, PartyNextDoor and Yeat.
In all, nine new tracks are peppered throughout the video, including Drake's highly anticipated remix of Ella Langley's smash hit Choosin' Texas.
And if that wasn't enough of a head rush for Drake fans, at the Toronto premiere of FOMO on Tuesday, the rapper known as "6 God" revealed he's planning to hit the road again in 2027 for a world tour.
"There are some other things on the horizon, some big shows," he said, nonchalantly.
Unfortunately for fans who missed Tuesday's livestream, their fears of missing out became a reality: Drake made the film private on his YouTube page shortly after its debut.
Reaction online from those who did catch it was mixed.
One user on X wrote, "Welp… I can honestly say ya'll didn't miss out on 'FOMO' if you haven't seen it yet unless watching Drake dance & looking unserious is your thing."
Another user gave a far more glowing review, saying the film was "a symbol of longevity and consistency" and "a well deserved pat on the back for his 20 year long career in music."

Jamaican dancehall artist Spice extended congratulations to her friend on Instagram, posting a video of the pair with a caption which said, in part: "Congratulations @champagnepapi WOW "FOMO" left me speechless. The amount of hardwork, dedication, and passion you've poured into fomo is truly remarkable."

items: Drake's producer Boi-1da says rapper 'always bounces back'

blocks.text: Drake, whose real name is Aubrey Graham, sent fans into a frenzy when he began hinting at his latest rollout last month. He first shared old pictures of his family on Instagram, captioning the carousel "FOMO 2026," then followed it two weeks later with a picture of a CD cover with the words "Fear of Missing Out."
The day before the release, the Champagne Papi teased the drop with a grainy image of himself, alongside a lengthy, reflective caption describing the film as "self-funded surrealism".
He described the video as "a story about making the absolute most of it all in one summer" and shared some "advice" to people before they watched it.
"Nobody is coming to save you," he said. "You must use each day to decipher who you love and trust and march forward with them."

He shared his hopes that the video would "serve as motivation to make that call, take that trip, drop that song, open that shop, see your parents, leave that relationship or stay in it forever, spend that bread, get some more, etc."
He also challenged those who "keep saying our genre is dying" and "nobody is watching nobody is listening."
"I still care … so be kind and rewind."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kayla McLean is a web journalist with CBC News in Toronto. She grew up in Brampton, Ont., and received her bachelor of arts in media production at Toronto Metropolitan University. Before joining CBC in 2024, she worked as a breaking news reporter at Global News Toronto — covering everything from crime, sports, festivals and politics. She also reported for Global News's current affairs show, The New Reality, covering stories with a focus on racial equality and climate justice. She also previously held positions as a chase producer and writer for CTV News Channel.

articles.title: Key House Democrat refuses to clear Trump’s $2.8bn arms sale to Israel
articles.summary:
Pro-Israel Gregory Meeks raises concerns over threat to civilian lives from package of 40,000 one-ton bombs

The top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee has thrown up a roadblock…

blocks.text: The top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee has thrown up a roadblock to one of the largest US arms transfers of Trump’s second term, refusing to clear a $2.8bn sale of 2,000lb bombs to Israel.
Gregory Meeks announced the hold on Tuesday on a package of 40,000 of the bombs, among the most destructive conventional munitions in the US arsenal.

“The Trump administration has not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with US law and with appropriate protections for civilians,” he said. “I therefore will not clear this sale at this time.”
The deal, funded through US Foreign Military Financing, covers 20,000 MK-84 bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrator warheads.

Meeks cannot single-handedly veto the $2.8bn arms transfer, but his leverage comes from the informal custom of “tiered review”. Under this practice, the state department submits major weapons packages to top foreign affairs lawmakers for an informal sign-off before triggering a formal notification to Congress. Killing the sale outright would need a veto-proof joint resolution of disapproval in both chambers, a bar Congress has not cleared. A similar push by Senator Bernie Sanders failed along party lines in April.

In 2025, the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, declared a national security emergency to bypass congressional review and fast-track nearly $3bn in weapons, including more than 35,000 heavy bombs and 4,000 bunker-buster warheads. With a separate $6.67bn package in January, the administration has now cleared or expedited over $12bn in arms for Israel since Trump took office. Meeks has said the pace has outrun oversight, accusing officials of skipping briefings and rushing sales while raising alarms over Israeli conduct in the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.

The hold also lands amid longstanding accusations that Israel has used American weapons unlawfully. The Leahy laws bar US assistance to foreign military units credibly linked to extrajudicial killings and serious abuse; the state department in 2024 flagged at least five Israeli units on those grounds before the war in Gaza even began, including one battalion tied to the death of a Palestinian American at a West Bank checkpoint.

The Geneva conventions, meanwhile, bar arming a party where there is a clear risk of war crimes – a standard a UN commission of inquiry cited last year in finding Israel’s Gaza campaign amounted to genocide and calling on the US and other states to halt weapons transfers. In 2024, Biden administration lawyers, including some at the state department, had concluded it was reasonable to assess that Israel had violated international humanitarian law and Leahy laws by using American weapons in Gaza, even as the administration publicly avoided making that determination.
Meeks, long known for his strong pro-Israel views, emphasized that the hold was not a break with the country itself.

“This decision does not diminish congressional support for Israel’s legitimate defense needs,” he said. “It reflects Congress’s responsibility to ensure that US-funded weapons are used lawfully, responsibly and with meaningful safeguards for human life.”
The state department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt
articles.summary: Black - who had business ties to Epstein - declined to appear and provide documents related to the convicted sex offender.

blocks.text: The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying legal summons related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Black - who had business ties to Epstein - did not comply with a subpoena ordering him to appear before the House Oversight Committee earlier this month and share documents related to Epstein.
Lawyers for Black, who has sued over the summons, called the contempt move "outrageous".
After passage of the measure holding Black in contempt, Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said: "No one is above the law."
"We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors."
In a statement shared with US media, lawyers for Black called the House move an "outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr. Black".

"The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer," they said.
The measure, which passed by unanimous consent, means the matter will be referred to the US justice department, which will decide whether to criminally prosecute Black.
In a statement, the committee's top Democrat, Congressman Robert Garcia, called the contempt vote "an important step towards justice and accountability".
"We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," he said.
Black walked out of voluntary testimony before the House Oversight Committee in June after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time.
Black left Apollo Global Management, which he co-founded, amid scrutiny in 2021 over his Epstein ties. He has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein.
The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June.
Black has said he hired Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling lawmakers in June that he gave Epstein $158m (£118m) for legitimate reasons.
The billionaire has said he did not know about Epstein's crimes until he was charged with sex trafficking in July 2019.

articles.title: How do you take T. rex's temperature? These scientists did it
articles.summary: Scientists have long discussed whether and which dinosaurs were warm-blooded. Now, researchers say they have used chemistry to take the temperature of two T. rexes. Here's what they found.

image.caption: Thomas the Tyrannosaurus rex can be seen at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County. Two of his teeth were used in this analysis to determine the body temperature of T. rexes. (Dinosaur Institute, Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County)

blocks.text: Science·New
Scientists have long discussed whether and which dinosaurs were warm-blooded. Now, researchers say they have used chemistry to take the temperature of two T. rexes. Here's what they found.
Chemistry provides 'compelling' evidence that T. rexes were warm-blooded
Scientists have long discussed whether and which dinosaurs were warm-blooded. Now, researchers say they have used chemistry to take the temperature of two T. rexes.

It wasn't easy, acknowledged Aradhna Tripati, a professor and geochemist at the University of California, Los Angeles. She co-authored the research published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances, and explained it to CBC's Quirks & Quarks ahead of an interview with host Bob McDonald.
"You would not want to go to a T. rex and stick a thermometer in its mouth or in its armpit or in its butt, you know, the way you might take temperature in a person or most other animals."
Nor could you, considering they went extinct about 66 million years ago.
How you take the temperature of an extinct animal
Instead, scientists used a technique that relies on chemistry that varies with temperature, and leaves signals in certain hard tissues such as tooth enamel and eggshells.

Those materials contain a mineral called bioapatite, where carbon atoms bond with oxygen. A heavier kind of carbon atom (carbon-13, which has one more neutron than carbon-12) bonds preferentially with a heavier, rarer kind of oxygen atom (oxygen-18, rather than oxygen-16). This is more prevalent at lower temperatures, where the bonds are more stable.
By comparing the amount of "isotope clumping" in living animals with different body temperatures, scientists can estimate the body temperature of extinct animals, including dinosaurs.
In fact, UCLA scientists did that a decade ago using eggshells from titanosaurs and oviraptors, and concluded that they were both warm-blooded.
They had also analyzed teeth from some plant-eating dinosaurs, such as brachiosaurs, which have thick enamel for grinding plants.
How hot was Thomas the T. rex?
But tyrannosaurs have very thin tooth enamel, Tripati said, so getting enough tooth enamel for the analysis was tricky.
The researchers worked on the technique with more common teeth from the megalodon, an ancient giant shark, until they could successfully do the analysis with very small samples.
Then they requested some tooth enamel from Thomas the tyrannosaur, a young adult T. rex skeleton displayed at the L.A. County Natural History Museum.

"They wouldn't let us pull a tooth off and just, you know, destroy it," Tripati recalled. But the scientists were permitted to shave a little bit off the sides of two teeth – "a pinch of salt amount."
They also managed to get a T. rex tooth fragment from a specimen identified only by a number.

By analyzing the three teeth, the researchers estimated T. rex's body temperature at between 33.8 C and 38.8 C – similar to that of large mammals such as elephants and large and possibly flightless birds such as ostriches (which have temperatures between 38.1 C and 39.7 C), but lower than that of smaller birds that can fly, which tend to have body temperatures between 41.1 C and 42.1 C.
What this means for tyrannosaurs of the north
Tripati says an animal's body temperature affects its behaviour and where it can live.
"A warm blooded T. rex is ... a T. rex that can go almost anywhere on the continent, including the Arctic. That's a very different animal from a sun-basking reptile."

Anthony Fiorillo, a paleontologist who described a tiny tyrannosaur in Alaska a decade ago, said while predators like T. rex were speculated to have warmer body temperatures, "this paper makes a solid and compelling case." Fiorillo, executive director of the New Mexico Museum of Natural History, added in an email that it provides "food for thought" about how dinosaurs may have adapted to life in the far north.
New 'reaper of death' tyrannosaur is the oldest found in Canada

François Therrien, curator of dinosaur paleobiology at the Royal Tyrrell Museum in Alberta, was part of a team that used isotope clumping to analyze the eggshells of small, meat-eating dinosaurs called troodons, and found they were as warm-blooded as birds with body temperatures more than 40 C.
He said researchers knew that tyrannosaurs grew fast and weren't just sluggish, cold-blooded animals, but this study provides a more precise, confident measure of body temperature.

The fact that it had such a warm body temperature suggests T. rex could be active during the day, at night and in winter, said Therrien, and explains how tyrannosaurs could range from Mexico to Alaska, and could have crossed the Bering Strait between Asia and North America in the far north, as there's evidence they did.

However, Therrien is not sure T. rex had quite the same kind of warm-blooded metabolism as modern mammals and birds do, which may have required more food than the ecosystem could support, given their size: "That's still subject to debate."

articles.title: ‘Made in Europe’ laws could derail UK plans for reset with EU
articles.summary:
Government sources say legislation aimed at China poses a risk to British businesses and must be addressed

European legislation that threatens to lock British business out of EU industry…

blocks.text: European legislation that threatens to lock British business out of EU industry could derail a planned reset summit between the bloc and the UK, government sources have said.

The “Made in Europe” legislation – formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act – is designed to curb China’s increasing presence in European industry, but was not on the reset plan agreed by the former prime minister, Keir Starmer, and the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, in London in May 2025.

A follow-up summit was due to be held in July this year, but was cancelled after Starmer’s resignation. The government is now looking to change the agenda, with one source saying that “Made in Europe should be on the agenda”.

It is understood that Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister with responsibility for the reset, told the EU’s trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, this was the UK’s new priority when the pair met last week.

On Tuesday, the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, told a gathering of UK business leaders on Tuesday they needed to let their EU partners know the risks posed by Made in Europe, which will prioritise EU suppliers in key industries including car manufacturing and defence.

Ministers have privately expressed fears that the reset has lost significant momentum since Andy Burnham became prime minister, with his focus on the domestic agenda. Agreements have yet to be reached on several key issues, including what tuition fees will be paid by EU students coming to the UK on a mooted “youth experience” programme.

blocks.caption: Keir Starmer and Ursula von der Leyen set out plans for a UK-EU reset in London in May 2025. Photograph: Carl Court/PA

blocks.text: UK sources say that while a food and drink deal and a youth mobility scheme are still on the agenda, the government will not agree to a new summit date until the bigger issues of the Industrial Accelerator Act are included in discussions.
There was talk in London and Brussels that a meeting could be convened on 6 November, but it is understood this could now be pushed backuntil the end of November or beyond.

One government source said: “We are willing to negotiate on the things that matter to them, but they have to be able to negotiate the thing that matters to us. Made in Europe should be on the table, definitely.”
The UK fears the Made in Europe laws could jeopardise billions of pounds worth of trade if British goods are not categorised as European, locking it out of key contracts on the continent.
France, which conceived the Made in Europe laws, is pushing to have the legislation passed by the end of the year, deepening fears that British manufacturing could be left behind.

It is thought that France is sympathetic to the UK’s position, but believes increasing competition from China makes it more important to get the legislation on the books now, and make allowances for third countries later, a process that could take years.

blocks.caption: A Chinese-made electric bus on the streets of Copenhagen, Denmark. Photograph: Francis Joseph Dean/Dean Pictures/Alamy

blocks.text: One EU diplomat said that there was substantial backing among key member states for the UK to be included in Made in Europe, though not all agreed.
“The problem is the benefits are seen as asymmetrical,” the diplomat said. “The UK gets more out of it than the EU.”
It is understood the Netherlands, Germany, Poland and Italy are all in favour of the UK’s inclusion, but France remains unconvinced.
The government’s newly assertive approach could give the UK some leverage in negotiations over concessions on youth mobility, something that is a political priority for many EU capitals.
Another UK source said a deal on Made in Europe would be “a good faith demonstration that we can find answers and almost everything else”.
A government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.
“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”
The UK’s desire for a deal on manufacturing rules comes at time when the EU is under pressure from industry across the bloc to loosen China’s growing presence in supply chains.
after newsletter promotion
Last week, manufacturing bosses warned of a potential loss of 300,000 jobs this year unless incentives are put in place to make European products more attractive than cheaper parts from China.
The EU’s deficit with China is now running at €1bn a day, with fears that European companies are being cannibalised from within.
In her state of the union address to the European parliament on Wednesday, Von der Leyen said the EU needed to grow non-Chinese supplies of rare earths and critical minerals vital to manufacturing.
Her surprise offer of an associate membership deal with Canada demonstrated how far Brussels can go to court third country partners.

Speaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, the EU chief said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships.”

The EU and Canada are due to hold a summit in late October to develop their future relationship. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, though it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, enabling deep economic integration with these countries, which follow many EU rules including free movement – a red line for the UK.
Carney, who is due to address the European parliament on Thursday, has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU, as his country seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.

blocks.caption: Mark Carney and Andy Burnham in Liverpool on Wednesday night. Photograph: John Clifton/Action Images/Reuters

blocks.text: Burnham met Carney at a football match in Liverpool on Wednesday night, where the two Everton fans watched their team in the League Cup. Burnham is also due to meet the US president, Donald Trump, for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York next week.

The potential new alliance between the EU and Canada will worry UK ministers that the bloc’s priorities are shifting. Should Burnham fail to complete a food and drink deal that was already on Starmer’s reset agenda, it could have implications for October’s budget, as the economic effects of easing trade with the EU is priced in as part of growth calculations.
The Conservatives criticised the UK/EU reset on Wednesday, saying a future Tory government would build a wholly independent regulatory system.
Alex Burghart, the party’s deputy leader, and Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, warned the plans would make Britain less competitive.
Speaking at the Policy Exchange thinktank, Burghart said: “Labour’s EU reset is the worst of both worlds and will leave Britain unable to take advantage of our country’s future growth potential.
“The next Conservative government would not be bound by this arrangement and will begin work now on a genuinely independent regulatory system.”

articles.summary: Fencing went up Wednesday around the main Kennedy Center building, a day after the Trump-aligned board voted to close most of the performing arts centre for repairs.

image.caption: Fencing is placed outside the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on Wednesday. (Nathan Ellgren/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
Fencing went up Wednesday around the main Kennedy Center building, a day after the Trump-aligned board voted to close most of the performing arts centre for repairs.
Centre's board voted to close after judge blocked return of Trump's name to institution
That vote came after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning U.S. President Donald Trump's name to the building.

The Republican president had said in a social media post that the closure was needed for safety repairs. But he said the repairs, which Congress has allocated $257 million US to cover, would only happen if the board was permitted to move forward with plans to add his name to the building.

Activists who have opposed the closure said there has been no vehicle or pedestrian access to the building. An Associated Press reporter who approached the main building was told by a security guard that it was closed.
Fears of 'a wrecking ball'
Laura Bligh, who has attended protests with the advocacy group Hands Off the Arts, said she feared some or all of the building may be torn down before a legal case is concluded.
"The worst case scenario is a wrecking ball," she said, adding that the Trump administration can't be trusted because "look what they did to the East Wing."
White House construction crew demolishes part of East Wing

The administration demolished the East Wing of the White House and is replacing it with a massive ballroom. Trump also plans to build a triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery and is eyeing a golf course renovation along the Potomac River.

The Kennedy Center board voted in August to inscribe his name on the Kennedy Center's facade so it would read "The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump." If the Trump Kennedy Center Fund reached $100 million US, another inscription would be added reading "Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund."
The plaza in front of the Kennedy Center would also be renamed in Trump's honour.
Board proposals shot down by judge
All of those proposals were shot down Tuesday by U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who ruled that nothing could happen "without Congress's blessing."

Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, requested an emergency court hearing Wednesday regarding what she called Trump's "unlawful closure of the Kennedy Center." Beatty has led efforts to block Trump's name from being added to the building, and had a verbal confrontation with Trump Tuesday during a virtual board meeting.

A staff member for a legal team representing Beatty was denied entrance to the building on Wednesday, Beatty's lawyer said in a court filing. The staffer "was informed by several security staff members that the building is currently closed to the public," the filing said.

The staff member also was informed that construction is beginning on the building's interior and that the public is completely barred from accessing the facility for "safety reasons," the filing said, adding that the nature of the construction activities and any potential demolition are unclear.

"Given the unexplained and unlawful closure, it is possible Defendants intend to undertake immediate steps in order to make public access practically impossible for the foreseeable future, including by demolishing public avenues of access to the building, and thereby evade the court's order," the filing said.
Roma Daravi, a spokesperson for the Kennedy Center, did not respond to requests for comment. But she wrote on social media that the building must be closed for safety reasons.

"Compounding systemic infrastructure failures from decades of neglect have left a crumbling building and safety concerns require an immediate closure of @TKCOfficial main building," she wrote on X. "Chairman @realDonaldTrump continues to support this great American institution while legal battles halt the progress to save it."

And so here we are. This statement from Trump blows my mind. That a sitting president would not let any renovations to a public building go on unless he gets to first put his name in the said building… What a sad state of affairs. What a tragedy. Actually, how small minded, how… pic.twitter.com/FlZl5ifWxs—mariashriver
Maria Shriver, John F. Kennedy's niece and former first lady of California, called the standoff over the name "a sad state of affairs" and a "tragedy."
She said in a post on X that it appears Trump "will not rest until his name is permanently connected to the name of a great president, whose memory this building was dedicated to."
"Imagine spending your days focused on this, while a war rages under your leadership," she added.

articles.title: Diver injured in great white shark attack off Quebec's Gaspé coast
articles.summary: A diver was transported to hospital after being injured by a great white shark in Percé, Que., in the province’s Gaspé region.

image.caption: According to the Canadian Shark Attack Registry, 15 confirmed shark-related incidents have been recorded in Canada over more than 330 years. (Kirk Yang)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
A diver was transported to hospital after being injured by a great white shark in Percé, Que., in the province’s Gaspé region.
Incident comes amid increase in great white shark sightings in the Gulf of St. Lawrence
According to the Canadian Coast Guard, the incident occurred shortly before 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday.
“Emergency response measures were initiated immediately,” Plongée Percé, a commercial diving firm, said in a Facebook post Wednesday.
“The individual involved received first aid on site before being quickly transported to hospital for further evaluation. We have confirmation that their life is not in danger.”

The Canadian Coast Guard confirms the victim was aboard the vessel Yoda, a Canadian Coast Guard Auxiliary dive boat. As of Wednesday afternoon, the organization was unable to confirm the nature of the victim’s injuries.
On Facebook, Plongée Percé thanked those who helped with the rescue and said it was suspending diving activities for the rest of the season.
Increase in great white sightings
Over the summer, great white shark sightings became more frequent in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and off the coasts of the Gaspé Peninsula and the Magdalen Islands.

Four of these sharks — Webster, Ernst, Bella and Nori — are being tracked by Ocearch, a global non-profit organization that helps scientists study sharks. Nori was spotted south of Anticosti Island, while Ernst and Bella are swimming northeast of the Magdalen Islands.

The organization told CBC News in August that the sighting of Webster off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador was a sign of a healing ocean. Webster is a 12-foot shark weighing just over 1,000 pounds.

Ocearch founder Chris Fischer said the population of great white sharks was nearly decimated from the 1970s to the 1990s. He said only around nine per cent of the global population remained before efforts were made to protect the remaining population.
Having sharks in the region is a good sign for local fisheries, he said, as sharks instinctively put pressure on seals and ultimately protect fish stocks.

items: Does Nova Scotia need shark-detecting drones?
Shark sightings off northern Newfoundland a welcome sign for researcher

blocks.text: Caroline Miri, a marine biologist with Fisheries and Oceans Canada, said sharks play a key role at the top of the marine food chain.

“They're very important to the health and stability of our oceans and marine ecosystems because these sharks help keep in check some populations of invasive species, and they also control competing fish species lower down on the food chain,” Miri said.
Fischer said Ocearch has tagged around 115 sharks across the Atlantic, from Florida to Newfoundland and Labrador.

According to the St. Lawrence Shark Observatory, the recent increase in sightings of great white sharks in the gulf is mainly due to better documentation and a recovery of the species, which was considered endangered in Canadian waters.
According to the Canadian Shark Attack Registry, 15 confirmed shark-related incidents have been recorded in Canada over more than 330 years.
Written by Isaac Olson, with files from Radio-Canada

articles.title: Trump's Chief of Staff Susie Wiles announces she's cancer-free
articles.summary: The 69-year-old White House chief of staff is a powerful figure and particularly close to the US president.

blocks.text: White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles has announced she is free of cancer, exactly six months after she announced her diagnosis.
In a post on X, Wiles said her pathology tests "came back clear" after a visit to the Mayo Clinic earlier this week.
Wiles, 69, is considered among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president.
In her post, Wiles thanked Trump for his "unwavering support" and vowed to continue working to "advance his America First Agenda".
Wiles continued working virtually at the White House during the six months of treatment following her diagnosis.
In a March statement, Wiles said that one in eight women are diagnosed with breast cancer.
"Every day, these women continue to raise their families, go to work and serve their communities with strength and determination," she said. "I now join their ranks."
Her post on Wednesday did not reveal any more details about her treatment.
Wiles is the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff - widely considered to be the most important role in the White House.
In her position, Wiles works to keep the president's agenda on track and serves as a gatekeeper to President Trump, as well as a policy coordinator and political advisor.
Before taking the job, Wiles played a significant role in President Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.
Her tenure, however, has not been without controversy.
In December, Vanity Fair published interviews with Wiles in which she gave a blunt - and occasionally unflattering - assessment of her time working in the Trump White House.
For example, she described the famously teetotaling president as having an "alcoholic's personality" but added that there's "nothing he can't do. Nothing, zero, nothing."
She also provided candid thoughts about other figures close to the US president, describing Vice-President JD Vance as a "conspiracy theorist" and Elon Musk as an "odd, odd duck."

The US president, however, swiftly came to her defence and Wiles described Vanity Fair's reporting as having omitted "significant context" to create a "chaotic and negative narrative" about the administration.
President Trump and the White House have yet to comment on Wiles' announcement.

articles.title: U.S. Federal Reserve raises interest rates for 1st time in 3 years
articles.summary: The Federal Reserve said it cut rates to help bring inflation back to the central bank's two per cent target. It's the first policy shift under the new Fed chief, who took office in late May after…

image.caption: Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference at the Federal Reserve in Washington, in July. (Mark Schiefelbein/Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business·New

The Federal Reserve said it cut rates to help bring inflation back to the central bank's two per cent target. It's the first policy shift under the new Fed chief, who took office in late May after being selected by Trump with an expectation that he would ‌cut rates. But economists say those pressures aren't hitting Canada in quite the same way, and don't put the same kind of pressure on the Bank of Canada.
The Fed was widely expected to raise interest rates ahead of the decision

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate Wednesday for the first time since 2023 in an effort to quell stubbornly high inflation, a move that could spur a sharp response from the White House.

The quarter-point increase lifts the Fed's key rate to about 3.9 per cent and, over time, could result in higher borrowing costs for American mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards. In a set of quarterly projections, the Fed also signalled that its rate-setting committee expects to hike rates a second time later this year, to 4.1 per cent.
"Today's policy action will support a timelier return" to the central bank's two per cent inflation goal, the Fed said in a statement.
The move comes as Americans are already struggling with high costs for groceries, gas and housing. Affordability has taken on a leading role in the upcoming midterm elections, just seven weeks away.

The rate hike is a surprising turnaround for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who was appointed by U.S. President Donald Trump and took over the top job in May. While under consideration by Trump last year, Warsh often suggested the Fed could reduce its key rate, echoing the president's call for lower borrowing costs.

And in April, when Warsh's nomination was under consideration by the Senate Banking Committee, Trump said in a television interview that he would be disappointed if Warsh didn't cut rates. On the same day, however, Warsh told the committee he had not promised Trump he would cut rates and said he would be "an independent actor" as Fed chair.
Will Bessent's bond market intervention make U.S. inflation worse? | About That

Yet the ongoing disruptions from the Iran war, which have pushed up average gas prices more than seven per cent from just a month ago, threaten to spread through the economy and keep broader inflation stubbornly high. An inflation report last week showed core prices, which exclude food and energy, accelerated slightly in August.
According to the Fed's preferred measure, inflation was 3.7 per cent in July compared with a year earlier.

Earlier Wednesday, the government said retail sales jumped 1.2 per cent in August from the previous month, a sign consumers are still spending at healthy levels despite sentiment surveys indicating Americans remain gloomy about the economy. Strong spending is a sign that interest rates at current levels aren't necessarily restricting the economy enough to cool inflation.

items: U.S. Senate votes to approve Trump's pick for Federal Reserve chair

blocks.text: "While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient," the Fed said, likely referring to ongoing consumer spending and strong investment in AI data centres by large technology companies.
Kevin Hassett, Trump's top economic adviser, was asked in an interview with Fox News on Sunday how Trump might react to a rate hike.
"I'm sure he's not going to be super happy about it, but he will defend the independence of Kevin Warsh above all," Hassett said.
More hikes are also possible. Wall Street investors have forecast three hikes in total, with additional increases in December and March.
Inflation is still a problem | Mind Your Business
Bank of Canada not facing same pressure: economist
The rate hike south of the border doesn't necessarily signal similar moves in Canada any time soon, according to economists.

The Canadian and U.S. central banks sometimes change interest rates in similar ways because the two economies tend to face the same challenges, explains Paul Beaudry, a professor at UBC's Vancouver School of Economics and a former deputy governor at the Bank of Canada.

items: Inflation risks rise with higher fuel costs and new U.S. tariffs, Bank of Canada governor warns

blocks.text: Right now, Canada is also facing rising inflation driven by rising energy prices because of the war in Iran. The pace of inflation held steady at three per cent in August — above the Bank of Canada's two per cent target.

But Beaudry says the inflation problem in the U.S. is worse. Core measures of inflation that strip out volatile items like energy and food are at about 2.4 per cent in the U.S., compared with closer to two per cent in Canada.
"There's more inflation underlying in the U.S. So the U.S. has more to do to try to bring it back … to two per cent," Beaudry said.

Canada's economy is also weaker by comparison, Beaudry points out, partly because tariffs and higher unemployment. All things considered, that means Canada doesn't face the same pressure to raise rates.

A recent RBC Economics forecast update made the same case, saying Canada and the U.S. were both facing inflation pressures and rising bond yields, but were "entering these shocks from different starting points."
For that reason, they predicted the U.S. would raise rates in September but does not expect the Bank of Canada to raise rates until 2027.
With files from CBC's Abby Hughes

articles.title: Is EU’s offer to Canada a blueprint for Britain – or a reminder it is out in the cold?
articles.summary:
Ursula von der Leyen has opened door for Canada to become associate member to deepen links in ‘openly hostile world’

Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer…

blocks.text: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer alignment with “middle powers” since January in the face of recklessness in Washington.
But what should worry another middle power, the UK, is that it was Brussels that came up with Wednesday’s big reveal in Strasbourg.

To a standing ovation at her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted to open the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first “associate member” in a push to forge new ⁠links among allies in “an openly hostile world“.
The European Commission president’s deal could be seen as an “earthquake” offer said Joel Reland, of UK in a Changing Europe, thought it remains “deliciously vague”.
But it also sets Canada apart from the UK, which could, once upon a time, have had some sort of associate membership with the EU were it not for the drive for a clean break Brexit.
The last time associate membership of the EU was mooted was in relation to Ukraine as an off-the-books novel way of bringing Kyiv closer to the bloc without become a fully fledged member state.
New partnerships, von der Leyen said, were needed “in the cold fragility of today’s world” and in the face of an increasingly assertive China.

Just moments earlier she spoke about the need for the EU to diversify urgently its supply of critical raw materials and rare earths currently dominated by China allowing it to follow Japan and stockpile said minerals needed for everything from the car to the defence industries.
It is not a new subject – after all the EU has been grappling with China’s export surplus since 2023 and it introduced the Critical Raw Materials Act as far back as 2024.
The prospect of an enhanced relationship with Ottawa is one that Keir Starmer might have dreamed of.

Canada has something the EU desperately needs – rich supplies of CRM and rare earths – and the EU has something Canada urgently wants: new market for products it can no longer sell into the EU in the face of a trade war with Donald Trump.

Speaking before von der Leyen’s speech, Tobias Cremer, a German social democrat MEP, said a new deeper relationship between the EU and Canada could be a blueprint for other countries, including the UK.

Bernd Lange, the influential chair of the European parliament’s international trade committee, said associate membership could “become a model for close transcontinental partnerships with democratic countries against the new model of the law of the strongest”.

After Iceland’s rejection of membership of the EU, Fabian Zuleeg, the chief executive and chief economist of the European Policy Centre, suggested it was time that the EU developed new models, beyond the European Economic Area, that might offer “partial, gradual or associated membership options”.
after newsletter promotion
Reland said the vagueness of the offer extended to Canada could be promising for the UK’s hopes for a similar offer.

“Any deep Canadian integration into the EU market would take some very heavy work to negotiate a defined set of treaty-bound rights and obligations, and so it seems more likely that – at least in the short term – cooperation will focus on more vaguely constructed alliances for ‘prosperity’ and ‘security’,” which aligns with the UK government’s desires, Reland wrote on Wednesday.

In the current political climate in the UK, it is difficult to envisage a world in which Andy Burnham would encourage any associate membership of the EU. He has a steely focus on domestic issues and it keen to avoid going down any Brexit wormholes.
The UK is seeking a reset with the EU, but the goals in the first year were modest and have yet to be achieved.
The offer to Canada suggests the bigger ambitions for relations with the EU the better.
Additional reporting: Jennifer Rankin

articles.title: English far-right extremist who discussed killing Jews, Muslims and migrants is jailed
articles.summary:
Ivan Jennings, 46, sentenced to five years after pleading guilty to encouraging terrorism on social media

A rightwing extremist who discussed poisoning Jews and Muslims and called for the…

blocks.text: A rightwing extremist who discussed poisoning Jews and Muslims and called for the killing of migrants and minority communities has been jailed.

Ivan Jennings, 46, called for the murder of hundreds of people he labelled “subhumans”, saying it was “justified and actually needed”, in extreme far-right groups over a period of three months in 2024.

The father-of four from Stafford had pleaded guilty to encouraging terrorism in an online chat between 15 August and 14 November that year and dissemination of a terrorism publication, namely a manifesto by the Norwegian mass murderer Anders Breivik, on 21 August 2024.
Jennings, who worked at a warehouse, was jailed for five years and three months and handed a further five years on extended licence at Leicester crown court on Wednesday.
Daniel Oscroft, prosecuting, told the court that Jennings had been an “active participant” in at least seven extreme rightwing groups on the social media platform Telegram.

Jennings, who joined the far-right organisation Patriotic Alternative in early 2024, told one of the groups that he was in touch with a man “who wanted to go in a boat and make a difference to the amount of people coming into the UK”, the court heard.
In another post, when asked if he supported murder, the defendant wrote: “It’s not murder because we are at war. If it’s subhumans, it’s justified and actually needed.”

On 22 August that year, he searched online for motorboat chartering services at Dover and how much it cost to hire a boat in the UK. A week later, another user shared a video of a boat, on which Jennings commented: “We need one of those to take out the dinghy divers.”
He told another chat group “something needed to be done soon” and each person “needs to take out at least 200 and stop the constant influx [of migrants]”.
The defendant also shared a post about an event in Manchester celebrating Pakistan’s independence day, identifying it as a target with the message: “We need to start acting.”
He made reference to the 51 people killed in the Christchurch terror attacks, a mass shooting at two mosques in New Zealand on 15 October 2019, adding: “We need a bigger impact.”

The court heard that another user commented on the post about the Pakistan independence day event: “It disgusts me to see that in the UK.” Jennings replied: “Exactly, we need to start acting to turn the tables.”
after newsletter promotion
In another comment about the Pakistan event, he wrote: “If I go to prison for anything, it’s going to be for making a real change.”
Oscroft told the court: “In a smaller group of eight participants, there was discussion about the most poisonous mushrooms and how to get them into the food of Jews or Muslims.”

The defence barrister Oliver Renton said Jennings was “struggling with deep existential fears about himself” after he collapsed at work in 2023 in cardiac arrest, and that he descended into “fear and isolation” and became susceptible to “nihilistic, bleak worldviews”.
In his sentencing remarks, Judge Lockhart KC said Jennings had “deeply held abhorrent and racist views”.
