articles.title: Global Gender Gap Report: Women's hard-won gains 'fragile'
articles.summary: Two decades of progress toward gender parity is at risk as women's political representation declines, according to a new World Economic Forum report. At the current pace, the remaining gap could take…

image.caption: Women make up less than a third of lawmakers in the US CongressImage: J. Scott Applewhite/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Global Gender Gap Report 2026, published by the World Economic Forum (WEF) on Wednesday, reveals that gender parity worldwide is closer than ever — standing at 69.2%.
However, the Geneva-based nonprofit warned that full parity may still be 120 years away and that the progress made so far remains "fragile."

The report, which looked at gender parity across workforce participation, education, health and politics in 145 economies, found that women now occupy senior leadership positions in government and business at levels that were rare globally when the index began in 2006.

Yet, while women's presence at the top of politics has grown since the first report, the past decade has seen that trend reverse. The percentage of countries led by women peaked in 2022 and has now fallen back to 2016 levels.
WEF Managing Director Saadia Zahidi warned that while parity is a foundation for growth and competitiveness, it is "not inevitable."

"To accelerate, governments and employers need to learn from the policies that work and apply them faster. A new economy demands a new approach to talent," Zahidi said in a press release to accompany the report.
Bangladesh lacks women in politics
Women still missing in top power roles

The WEF found that women remain underrepresented in roles with the largest economic and political influence. They still hold fewer than a fifth of chief executive officer (CEO) positions, while only one in 10 ministerial roles held by women is considered high influence.
While the number of ministerial roles led by women has risen 26% since 2008, only one in 10 was considered weighty then — a share the WEF report said was "virtually unchanged today."

Despite nearly $1 trillion (€866 billion) being invested globally to develop artificial intelligence (AI), the report also revealed that fewer than one in five AI engineers are women and they are underrepresented at every level of AI firms.

For the 17th consecutive year, Iceland leads the ranking with 93% of the gender gap closed, followed by its Nordic neighbors Finland and Norway. The three nations have made the Top 10, along with Sweden, every year since 2006.
Namibia ranked fourth globally, higher than Germany (9th), the United Kingdom (5th) and Australia (8th).
US falls in gender gap ranking
The United States dropped five places in the rankings to 47th, with 74.9% of its gender gap closed.
The country achieved full parity in education for a second year — ranking first in the world in that area.
In the US, women have long matched men in professional and technical jobs, but parity in senior management has fallen by almost 11 points since 2006, the WEF calculated.

The political score fell 4.1 points from last year after the share of women ministers dropped from two-thirds parity to one-half. The decline coincided with a lower share of women serving as Cabinet secretaries in President Donald Trump's second administration.
The WEF kept the head-of-state indicator for the US at zero as the world's largest economy has never had a female president.

blocks.caption: Only 63 of 193 countries, including Japan, have ever had a woman as head of government, according to the United NationsImage: Minoru Matsutani/Jiji Press/picture alliance

blocks.text: India stuck while China moves up
India, the world's most populous country, remains at 131st in the rankings, with 64.5% gender parity closed.

The report noted India's overall gains amount to a 4.3 percentage-point rise since 2006, which the authors said was mostly due to educational achievement. Women's labor-market participation has barely moved over 20 years, the WEF noted.

India's economic parity score has varied significantly since the first report. Parity among professional and technical workers has almost doubled since 2006, to 49.9%. Among legislators, senior officials and managers, however, it is still only 13.1%.

In parliament, India has closed 16.1% of the gender gap, up seven points since 2006, while the share of women in long-serving Prime Minister Narendra Modi's cabinet has fallen recently, with parity slipping to 5.9% from a 30% peak in 2019.

China, meanwhile, rose seven places to 96th, closing 69.9% of its gender gap. Economic parity is its strongest pillar, at 72.3%, but politics has barely moved in 20 years, with women still accounting for only a fraction of ministers.
Namibia's rise in women's political power
Large jumps for Namibia, Kenya and Ghana
Reaching 84.5% parity in the latest report, Namibia leads the way in Sub-Saharan Africa, climbing four places to No. 4 in the ranking.

Namibia has long been well represented by women on the political stage. Last year, Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah became its first female president. The country also has a female vice-president and the parliament speaker is a woman, too.
Other African countries were among the biggest climbers in the 2026 rankings, with Kenya rising 33 places in a year to 65th, Ghana up 32 places to 56th and Angola climbing 30 places to 87th.
However, Africa shows the widest range of outcomes for women, the report found, with Chad recording the lowest score of 57.8% parity closed.
Other large climbers in the 2026 report were Guatemala, which rose 31 points to 50th place, and the Czech Republic, which climbed 25 points to 77th.
The WEF also ranked the countries that have progressed the most since 2006 in closing gender gaps, namely Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador, France, Guatemala, Iceland, Mexico, Namibia and Nepal.

articles.title: Tall athletes can't stretch their legs in container beds at Asian Games, official says
articles.summary: South Korea's delegation slams the wooden containers housing its athletes at the Asian Games in Nagoya city.

blocks.text: Wooden container huts meant for thousands of athletes have become the subject of heated criticism ahead of the opening of Japan's Asian Games on Saturday.
Jung Jae-yong, vice-president of the Korea Basketball Association, told AFP news agency the accommodation was the "worst it has ever been".
"Athletes who are over two metres (6ft 7in) tall cannot even stretch their legs out on the beds. It's unreasonable."

The Games, held in the city of Nagoya and wider Aichi prefecture, have faced weeks of concern about a potential shortage of beds. More than 17,000 athletes and officials are attending - exceeding the initial 15,000 expected.
The containers, which will be housing around 2,000 of the guests and are designed to be reused as disaster evacuation facilities, have been beset by complaints.
A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me."
Athletes were also briefly evacuated from the containers as record rainfall lashed Nagoya last week and caused widespread flooding. Water leakage was reported in some of the competition venues too.
Jung, the basketball official, told AFP that concerns over accommodation were shared by representatives from the other countries at the Games.
Indian authorities have built replicas of the huts to get their athletes used to living in them.
Accommodation manager Yuta Matsuo told Reuters the hosts were "fully aware of the dissatisfaction and concerns voiced by the athlete delegations".
They were "taking concrete steps to improve the environment for the athletes", he said.
Unlike the Olympic Games, where there is usually a designated athletes' village, organisers have opted to use temporary accommodation for competitors.
Beyond the container huts, between 4,000 and 5,000 participants will be staying on an Italian cruise ship which docked in Nagoya on Tuesday. The rest of the attendees will stay in hotels.
Initially, 15,000 athletes and officials had been expected to attend the Games.
But in mid-August the Olympic Council of Asia said the number would be closer to 17,000 after teqball - which combines elements of football and table tennis - and padel were included.

Hideaki Omura, president of the organising committee and Governor of Aichi Prefecture, previously said authorities had set aside a budget for 15,000 people and had "neither the manpower nor the budget to make the necessary arrangements" for the additional athletes.
"There is simply nowhere for them to stay. If they still wish to come, they will have to make their own arrangements."

But last month, organisers and the Olympic Council of Asia said all "17,000-plus" athletes and officials who had registered before the deadline in July have been provided with "Games-appropriate accommodation".
"The final preparations are all on track and progressing smoothly ahead of what promises to be the most spectacular Asian Games held for generations," their statement read.
Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham Tolentino told AFP that while all the country's athletes have secured a bed, some officials and coaches were staying in "different hotels and Airbnb".
Though basketball and football matches have already started, the Asian Games officially begin on Saturday and will end on 4 October.

articles.title: German drama 'Blindspot Berlin' revisits 2016 Christmas market attack
articles.summary: A decade after the terrorist attack on a Berlin Christmas market, a new miniseries looks into the institutional failures that allowed the deadly truck rampage to happen.

image.caption: The German miniseries 'Blindspot Berlin' premiered at the Toronto Film FestivalImage: Hubert Mican Jagd/NEUESUPER

blocks.text: A decade after the deadliest jihadist attack in Germany's history, a new six-part TV series looks at the institutional failures that allowed it to happen.

"Blindspot Berlin," which had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, follows the year-long police investigation that failed to stop Anis Amri — a Tunisian whose asylum applications had been rejected, and who was already known to German security services — from driving a hijacked truck into a crowded Christmas market at Berlin's Breitscheidplatz on December 19, 2016.

Twelve people died, including Lukasz Urban, the Polish driver Amri shot before seizing his vehicle. Dozens more were injured; a 13th victim died of their injuries in 2021. Amri fled the scene and made his way across Europe before being shot dead four days later by Italian police, near Milan, during a routine identity check.

"What happened behind the scenes of that attack is in many ways just as disturbing," says "Blindspot Berlin" director David Nawrath . "[It's] a picture of overwhelmed institutions, systemic failure and a staggering blindness to the threat that was developing right in front of our eyes."

blocks.caption: Along with the people who were killed, at least 56 more were injured in the truck attack Image: picture-alliance/dpa/M. Kappeler

blocks.text: Inside the Salafist network

Set in the year before the attack, the series follows police investigator Frank Laudin (Albrecht Schuch, of "System Crasher" and "All Quiet on the Western Front") and Isra Al-Husseini (Bayan Layla), a young officer and Arabic-language translator, as they try to infiltrate the Salafist network around Abu Walaa, the Iraqi preacher based in Hildesheim who recruited for extremist group "Islamic State" (IS). Frank recruits Murat (Tamer Trasoglu), who risks his life as an undercover informant. Inside the network, they find Amri: volatile, and getting more dangerous.

But despite repeated warnings, their bosses refuse to take the threat seriously. They dismiss Amri as a possible terrorist, in part because he is also a drug dealer, something the authorities see as incompatible with being a radical Islamist.
Fiction built on the parliamentary record

The series writers and production team closely based "Blindspot Berlin" on the facts of the Amri case, and the years-long parliamentary investigation into the institutional failures that made the attack possible. The main characters in the series — Frank, Isra and Murat — are fictionalized, but the events play out as they did in real life.

"We tried to keep as close as possible to what is known about the attack and what led to it," producer Simon Amberger told DW. "There is still a lot that isn't known, that is speculation. There we tried to leave things open."
Germany's Christmas markets open amid security concerns
Understaffed, uncoordinated, unheeded
The facts of the case are damning enough.

The parliamentary inquiry committee found that the criminal division investigating Amri and other suspects was grossly understaffed, that judicial and security agencies failed to coordinate the exchange of information, and that officials made serious errors of judgment. Amri's asylum claims were rejected, but he was never deported.

At one point the bureaucracy tipped into farce. Amri tried to leave Germany to rejoin his family and was stopped at the border, where police confiscated his passport on the grounds that he lacked the correct papers to go.
Not only a German story
The producers knew from the start that the story reached beyond Germany.

The Breitscheidplatz attack came at the end of a run of assaults across Europe: the Bataclan and coordinated shootings in Paris in 2015, the suicide bombings at Brussels airport and Maelbeek metro station, and a similar truck attack in Nice, in 2016.

blocks.caption: To prevent similar ramming attacks, security barriers are now installed around Germany's Christmas marketsImage: Jochen Tack/picture alliance

blocks.text: Despite the lessons learned in the past decade, threat levels remain high. On July 25, a man drove a van into the crowds of Christopher Street Day gay pride celebrations in Berlin, killing one and injuring dozens.

The Breitscheidplatz attack also continues to resonate today, as it raises questions on "how far a free democratic society is willing to go, how much of its freedom it is willing to sacrifice for security," says Amberger.
Fears of political misuse

He's aware, however, that a story of Islamic extremism, and the failure of the German state to protect its citizens, lands differently now, in the wake of recent elections that have seen a surge of support for the anti-immigrant, Islamophobic far-right AfD party.

"There is a danger that this story, this series, could be misused to support a simplistic, populist political agenda," Amberger admits. "But it isn't that simple. [In the series] we show how extremism arises in marginalized groups that feel isolated, unseen and powerless. The solution isn't 'stop immigration.'"
"Blindspot Berlin" premieres in Germany on public broadcaster ARD in October; its international distribution is also being planned.

articles.title: Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for serving dessert topped with ants
articles.summary:
Prosecutors sought jail term for chief executive of Evett after insects not approved for consumption were on menu

A South Korean court has fined the operator of one of Seoul’s most…

blocks.text: A South Korean court has fined the operator of one of Seoul’s most celebrated restaurants and its chief executive for serving a dessert topped with ants, an insect not approved for consumption under local food safety law.
The operator of Evett, a two-Michelin-star restaurant in the affluent Gangnam district, was fined 10m won (£5,400) and its chief executive 15m won, Newsis reported.
Prosecutors had sought a one-year prison term for the chief executive and a 20m wonfine for the company.

The judge at Seoul’s western district court, Lee Se-chang, said the offence was “by no means light”, citing the length of time the dishes had been sold for, the restaurant’s use of them to promote itself and tests that found heavy metals above permitted levels in the ants.

He said he had taken into account that the defendants admitted the offence, that the chief executive had no previous criminal record under the food safety law, that the number of ants served appeared lower than prosecutors had calculated and that the restaurant no longer used ants.
Ants are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, he said.
Both sides have seven days to appeal. The Guardian contacted Evett for comment.

Evett was founded by the Australian chef Joseph Lidgerwood, who has appeared on the Netflix cooking competition Culinary Class Wars and is the restaurant’s public face. He was not a defendant and was not charged.

Under South Korean food safety law, the legal duties fall on the person registered as operating the business. Ginny Kim, Lidgerwood’s wife, is registered as the company’s chief executive and was named as a defendant, alongside the company that operates the restaurant.
Only 10 insect species are approved as food ingredients in South Korea, including grasshoppers, mealworms and silkworm pupae.

Businesses wishing to use an unapproved insect must obtain temporary approval from the ministry of food and drug safety, a step the restaurant did not take. Violating the law carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison or a 50m won fine.
The ministry launched its investigation after seeing mentions of the ant dishes in blog posts and social media.

Prosecutors said the restaurant imported dried ants from the US and Thailand by post from April 2021, and served three to five of them atop a sorbet made with sikhye, a sweet Korean rice drink, until January 2025.
They estimated the dessert was served to 12,274 customers, using 49,096 ants, for total revenue of about 120m won.
Lawyers disputed that figure in court, arguing that only about 60% of customers accepted the ant topping when it was offered.

The restaurant also noted that only a small number of dishes on their 15-course menu included ants, and that restaurants in countries including Denmark, the UK and Australia use ants as an ingredient.
Insect-eating is neither new nor unusual in South Korea. Beondegi, steamed silkworm pupae, has been sold from street carts for decades and remains a nostalgic popular snack for children.

articles.title: Iranian security forces coordinated killing, torture and sexual abuse of protesters, says Amnesty
articles.summary:
Leaked documents and testimony reveal extent of regime’s crackdown in 2022 and how it paved the way for more brutal killings of protesters this year

Iranian security forces “coordinated” the…

blocks.text: Iranian security forces “coordinated” the killing, torture and sexual abuse of hundreds of people who took part in the women-led nationwide protests in September 2022, according to leaked state documents and interviews.

Tens of thousands of people, including children, took to the streets of towns and cities across Iran after the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, after her arrest by the “morality” police for allegedly not complying with the country’s hijab regulations.

In response, the Iranian state instigated a brutal crackdown. Official statements and leaked documents cited by Amnesty reveal instructions for a “firm and severe” response. One leaked order instructed forces to “respond mercilessly and go as far as causing death”.

The rights group has now investigated and verified the deaths of 377 protesters and bystanders, including 56 children. It also documented the cases of 16 people who were reportedly subjected to rape while arbitrarily detained in connection with the uprising, who included six women, seven men, a 14-year-old girl and two boys aged 16 and 17.

The Amnesty report said: “State agents penetrated women and girls vaginally, anally and orally, while men and boys were penetrated anally. Victims were penetrated with wooden and metal batons, glass bottles, hosepipes and/or the sexual organs and fingers of agents.”

The harrowing findings echo testimonies gathered by the Guardian during and after the crackdown. In a Guardian report from December 2022 medics said security forces were shooting female protesters in the faces, breasts and genitals, and warned that the severity of the injuries could leave hundreds of young Iranians with permanent damage.

blocks.caption: An X-ray of a woman shot in the crotch during Iran protests in 2022, with about 200 metal balls embedded in her upper thigh and pelvic area.  Photograph: supplied

blocks.text: In testimony published in 2023, a 25-year-old protester told the Guardian she had been blindfolded and sexually assaulted during interrogation by security agents. Similar testimonies involving sexual assault and torture were reported by people interviewed following the anti-regime protests that took place in January 2026.

Amnesty’s report says years of impunity for the violent crackdown paved the way for the even more brutal crackdown on the nationwide anti-government protests in January 2026, which culminated in the deaths of thousands of protesters over 48 hours on 8 and 9 January.

Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general, said: “This investigation exposes the layers of command and coordination behind the Iranian authorities’ deadly protest crackdowns. The agents on the streets operated within a hierarchical and coordinated chain of command linking them to officials who directed, enabled, facilitated and supported crimes committed on a massive scale.”
after newsletter promotion

Amnesty identified 87 Iranian officials, including the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, and Mohammad Bagheri, the former chief of the general staff of the armed forces, killed in an airstrike in June 2025, who it said should be investigated for “crimes against humanity”.

Amnesty also named the then minister of interior, Ahmad Vahidi, who has since become the general commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and the then deputy minister of interior for police and security, Majid Mirahmadi.

articles.title: L.A. driver arrested on murder charges after crashing SUV into bus, leading to fatal helicopter crash
articles.summary: A motorist was arrested on murder charges after authorities say she slammed her SUV into a city bus in Los Angeles, killing at least two people in that incident and injuring six others in a prelude…

image.caption: Flowers are placed at the scene of the news helicopter crash in L.A. Wednesday. (Ethan Swope/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

A motorist was arrested on murder charges after authorities say she slammed her SUV into a city bus in Los Angeles, killing at least two people in that incident and injuring six others in a prelude to a second deadly tragedy: the fiery crash of a TV news helicopter that was covering the collision.
A local news crew was in the chooper when it went down
3 people killed in L.A. news helicopter crash

A motorist was arrested on murder charges after authorities say she slammed her SUV into a city bus in Los Angeles, killing at least two people in that incident and injuring six others in a prelude to a second deadly tragedy: the fiery crash of a TV news helicopter that was covering the collision..

Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, of Simi Valley, was arrested Monday night and is being held at a Los Angeles jail with bail set at $4 million US, police said. The case is being forwarded to the district attorney's office, which will decide whether to file the charges in court or pursue different ones.
Information on a lawyer who could speak on her behalf was not immediately available.

The helicopter, which was used by NBC and Telemundo, crashed about two hours after police say Rios drove her 2004 Ford Expedition the wrong way down a busy avenue, ran a red light and struck a vehicle before hitting the bus. One passenger was fully ejected from the bus and another was partially ejected, police said.
Rios's mother, Cindy Rios, said she was shocked and saddened by the string of events. She said she had not spoken to Bailee Lynn since her arrest and had not been contacted by law enforcement.
"It's just horrible," Cindy Rios told The Associated Press in a phone interview Wednesday. "The fact that my daughter was involved and was the cause of it is just extremely disturbing."
"If anything, I'm sorry for the other families," she added. "My daughter's alive. People lost their lives."
News crew killed

Colleen Williams, an NBC4 Los Angeles anchor, confirmed during live broadcasts that two people on board the chopper were killed when the helicopter went down. At least one other person was killed on the ground, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department said.
"We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, process it," Williams said, her voice shaking with emotion. Moments later the coverage cut off.

Williams and the station's website identified those killed aboard the helicopter as Eliana Moreno, a familiar voice for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 during the station's aerial coverage, and pilot George Marciniw. Both were employees of Angel City Air, which operated the chopper.

Moreno, born in Orange County, joined the Angel City Air helicopter team in 2010, the same year she earned a broadcast journalism and political science degree from Chapman University. She reported for several Southern California news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, the NBC4 website said.
Marciniw grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.

items: TSB renews calls for updated helicopter safety rules following fatal northern Alberta crash
1 dead after plane crashes into 2 vehicles on B.C. road

blocks.text: "Losing five Angelenos is very painful," Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said. "And I know this community of Chatsworth, hit hard, will be grieving for some time."
At least four cars and two storage containers on the ground burned after the helicopter caught fire, which was quickly put out, according to officials.
"The helicopter itself, it's pretty well destroyed," fire spokesperson Capt. Branden Silverman said.
Two people were brought to a hospital, said Rico A. Gross, a fire department battalion chief. Their conditions were not immediately released.
NBC4 and Telemundo 52 Los Angeles said in a statement they "are deeply saddened" and extended "heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives."
California Gov. Gavin Newsom thanked the emergency crews responding to both crashes and said in a post on X that "our hearts are with the victims and families."
The U.S. National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said personnel will arrive Wednesday to begin an investigation into the cause of the helicopter crash.
There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the U.S. since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts.
Some have occurred during live broadcasts, including a midair collision of helicopters in Phoenix in 2007, and a deadly accident involving a Seattle news helicopter in 2000.

articles.title: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
articles.summary: The US president has pushed the issue to the forefront of American politics - even at the risk of losing supporters.

blocks.text: Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?
By
North America correspondent
According to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax.

It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.

Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.

The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.
None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will.

Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies.

"We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."

Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI.
"Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."
Watch: "Great" or "alarming" - Should AI be reined in?
According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."

A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.

It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.
Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.
But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?
The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AI

Trump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years.
According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.

The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.
Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.

Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind.
"We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."

The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.

Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.
Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to Trump

Trump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president.
"I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."

Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.
These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.
In Amodei's case, his conflicts over the Pentagon's unrestricted use of Anthropic's AI models could have negatively affected Trump's evaluation of Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development.

"This is the most prominent debate in the entire industry and has been since the beginning," said Matt Calkins, head of the tech firm Appian. "We knew it would spill into politics at some point because it had to."
Watch: AI needs a 'brake pedal', Anthropic co-founder tells BBC
Where the political debate goes from here is an open question.

With Trump's resistance, it is unlikely that Congress – despite promises of new hearings and proposed regulatory controls – will enact new legislation that Trump would sign into law. On Tuesday, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appeared to back away from earlier openness to congressional action, instead echoing Trump "AI hoax" rhetoric.

With midterm congressional elections looming, candidates running for office – both Republicans and Democrats – are wary of ending up on the wrong side of public opinion that, according to polls, is sceptical of the promised benefits of AI advances.
But Republicans are also wary of crossing Trump on an issue that has become a political touchstone for the president.

Even though the public is starting to pay attention, Calkins says that the issue has not yet become political dynamite, which means political rhetoric comes with little risk. The moment when AI warnings turn into a high-profile disaster, however, could be looming.
"It is possible that events in the future might electrify the public, and then positions - and talk - might not be so cheap," he said.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi drone south of Mecca
articles.summary: The Houthis deny targeting the Islamic holy city after the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen accuses them of a "disgraceful act".

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, according to the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.
Turki al-Maliki said the targeting of Mecca, which is the home of Islam's most sacred shrine and the focal point of the Hajj pilgrimage, was a "disgraceful act".

The 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation said attacks on Mecca and Medina province, where Islam's second holiest shrine is located, constituted an "unacceptable and intolerable transgression".
But the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen, denied targeting Mecca and accused Saudi Arabia of "fabrications and lies".

"There is no threat whatsoever from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and are far removed from the holy places," military spokesman Yahya Sarea said.
Sarea added that the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week.
He also said they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet over Marib province.

There was no immediate response from the Saudi-led coalition, but Maj Gen Maliki did say that its forces would "not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia and its hostile and terrorist behaviour".
On Tuesday, Saudi authorities issued a series of brief security alerts for incoming projectiles in a number of western areas, including Mecca and Jeddah, the kingdom's second largest city.

Meanwhile, the US embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a "reconsider travel" advisory, warning that Houthi attacks had targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic facilities and energy facilities.
The Houthis have recently seized control of large swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces.

Last week, they captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a key shipping route that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez canal.

The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

At the same time, Saudi Arabia's key East-West Pipeline, which was being used to transfer crude oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, had to be closed after it was badly damaged in a strike that the kingdom blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
Some experts have said it could take more than a month to repair the pipeline, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright predicted on Tuesday that oil should be flowing through it within days.

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner.
Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said.
A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability."

The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure.
Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains.
More than 90,000 people have been displaced in Yemen by the fighting between the Houthis and pro-government forces, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
"Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left," Amy Pope, the IOM's director general, warned last week.
The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Sunday that at least 500 people had been reported killed since the start of August, including 297 over the previous week.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title: How extreme weather is hurting the global economy
articles.summary: Heat waves, wildfires and floods have cascading economic impacts, causing incomes to decline and the price of basic goods to rise. The trend will escalate as temperatures continue to increase.

image.caption: We are already paying a price for burning fossil fuelsImage: Robin Utrecht/picture alliance

blocks.text: The last 11 years have been the planet's hottest on record. This changing climate is manifested in extreme weather events like heat waves and wildfires. But less obvious are the higher prices and lower wages linked to a heating world.

According to a 2026 study by the MIT Sloan School of Management and UCLA School of Law, climate change has already driven up average American household expenses by $900 (€780) a year — rising to above $1,300 for one in 10 US counties.

These costs would not exist in a world without climate change. They include escalating home insurance ($600 higher on average), increasing state and federal taxes due to disaster recovery costs or health impacts from wildfire smoke, for example.
"Climate inaction isn't just an environmental failure; it acts like a tax on every American household," wrote the researchers .

blocks.caption: An 8-month drought in California sparked catastrophic wildfires in 2025. But heat is also burning a hole in personal wealthImage: Mike Blake/REUTERS

blocks.text: How climate change is already hitting incomes

A 2024 report by Germany's Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact estimated that climate damages to agriculture, infrastructure, health and productivity could cost the world economy $38 trillion a year by 2050.
But how have climate-driven weather extremes already impacted salaries and household budgets?

"If we can't figure out what climate change is already costing us with the data we have, projecting the future becomes almost hopeless," said Derek Lemoine, an economics professor from the University of Arizona who has estimated a 12% reduction in US incomes as global temperatures have risen. This is also compared to a non-climate change scenario.
Lemoine shows how temperature extremes in one US county are having cascading economic impacts in distant locations with milder weather due to interconnected trade and supply chains.
"Much work studies climate change as if it changes weather in only one year and one location at a time," Lemoine told DW.

Instead, he wants to understand how, if a heat wave wipes out corn crops across America, other industries that rely on that corn, including livestock and food producers, will be impacted as the commodity becomes scarcer and increases in price.

blocks.caption: Drought-affected agriculture is having compounding economics impactsImage: Dragan Maksimović/DW

blocks.text: "As your costs have gone up," said Lemoine of producers impacted across the corn supply chain, "that's going to serve to make the income of everyone who depends on you go down."

Climate's impact on trade is also being felt in Germany, where record low water levels on the Rhine River, the busiest inland trade waterway in Europe, could shave as much as 0.2% off Germany's economic output in the third quarter of 2026, noted the Kiel Institute for the World Economy in July.

Prolonged dry weather linked to climate change is to blame as shipping capacity drops to as low as 15% on the river that connects Europe's largest port in Rotterdam in the Netherlands with much of western Germany.
Rhine River drops to record low levels, grounding ships
Compounding existing economic pressures
One Australian study also looks at how broad climate changes, rather than local shocks from single extreme weather events have gradually led to a decrease in productivity and economic output.

Timothy Neal, a researcher at the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales in Australia, co-authored the report showing that global heating reduced economic output in the state of NSW by an average of around 18%, or the equivalent of $21,288 Australian dollars (€12,974, $15,000) per person in 2024.
"The damage has already been quite severe," Neal told DW, adding that in a non-warming scenario, citizens would enjoy "lower food prices" and "lower poverty."

The report refers to droughts in parts of NSW in the mid-late 2010s that reduced productivity across the whole state by up to 10 billion Australian dollars due to lower agricultural yields and farm incomes, higher water costs and increased reliance on government assistance.
These financial impacts compounded through the state economy over time, influencing the cost of food, insurance and infrastructure maintenance.
In the words of the report, these effects also "compound existing economic pressures and contribute to widening disparities between regions," meaning an increase in income and wealth inequality.

blocks.caption: Putting planet-heating CO2 in the atmosphere is compounding economic stagnationImage: Stefan Ziese/imagebroker/IMAGO

blocks.text: Can climate adaptation limit costs?

"Climate change action should not be seen as a predominantly environmental but also economically sensible," said Frank Jotzo, an economist at the NSW Net Zero Commission, which works to decarbonize the state and commissioned the above study.

Referring to "defensive climate investments" such as reinforcing roads, railways and shipping infrastructure to adapt to a hotter world, Jotzo added that "if it wasn't for climate change, we could be putting that money and that effort into other things."
However, adaptation efforts such as the greening of cities to reduce heat island effects will be vital to head off much worse future economic impacts.
The 2026 European heat waves, for example, have already cost around €180 billion, which is the EU's entire projected economic growth for the year, according to one analysis.

Adaptation will also involve strengthening the hospital and medical system to counteract the health effects of heat waves that also reduce productivity as heat-stressed employees tire or struggle to sleep, Jotzo noted.

blocks.caption: Workers around the world are losing productivity due to extreme heatImage: Assad Hani/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: But Lemoine says that adaptation to climate-driven economic decline is so "costly in its own right" that it could exacerbate income loss and be ineffective if not done comprehensively.
Only when "all places" are insulated from weather extremes can the cascading economic impacts be addressed, he says.

Nonetheless, both adaptation and a rapid reduction of planet-heating emissions are together required to avoid climate-driven income loss that will worsen if warming outstrips Paris climate agreement targets.
"Unchecked climate change would create a permanent drain on wages and productivity," said Jotzo.
The economic cost of climate change and how to adapt

September 16, 2026
US bill sanctioning Russia could adversely impact India

India-US ties could come under pressure as the US lawmakers consider a Russia sanctions bill that would allow President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying Russian oil and gas. India, a major consumer of Russian energy, could be affected by the measure.

The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 cleared a key procedural hurdle in the House of Representatives on Tuesday in a 214-211 vote, media reports said. The House is expected to hold a final vote on Wednesday.
The bill, imposing sanctions on Russia's leadership, energy and defense sectors and "shadow fleet" accused of helping Moscow evade oil sanctions, was passed by the Senate last month.
If approved by the House, the bill would go to Trump to be signed into law.
The proposed tariffs seek toincrease economic pressure on Moscow by targeting countries that continue buying Russian energy.
India-US ties facing test

While India and Russia ties have grown stronger since the start of the war in Ukraine, driven largely by Russian oil exports, the same cannot be said of India-US relations under Prime Minister Narendra Modi as tensions mounted over New Delhi's purchases of Russian oil.
Last August, Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian imports over those purchases, on top of a 25% reciprocal tariff.
However, the additional Russia-related tariff was removed in February 2026, while the reciprocal tariff was reduced to 18% as part of a US-India trade framework.
However, the landmark bilateral trade agreement between the two countries remains in limbo, with no significant breakthrough.

The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed.
Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza.

articles.title: Kosovo ex-president Thaci sentenced to 25 years for war crimes
articles.summary: A Hague tribunal ruled that Hashim Thaci, a former leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), is responsible for war crimes carried out during the war of independence with Serbia.

image.caption: Hashim Thaci, 58, had said he expected an acquittal Image: Jerry Lampen/Reuters

blocks.text: A Kosovo war crimes tribunal on Wednesday found former President Hashim Thaci guilty of war crimes committed during the 1998-1999 war for independence from Serbia.
Thaci, a former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) commander, was sentenced to 25 years in prison for crimes including murder, torture and illegal detention.
He was tried along with three other former KLA guerrilla leaders in The Hague.
What did the tribunal rule?

The tribunal said Thaci was guilty of the murder of of 96 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces at the hands of the KLA during the conflict. He was also convicted for the illegal detention of 385 people and torturing more than 300 people
The court added Thaci had "actively participated in and encouraged crimes."
Prosecutors alleged KLA forces killed more than 100 political opponents and perceived collaborators with Serbian security forces during and just after the Kosovo war.
This included prisoners held at KLA facilities in Kosovo and Albania, along with politically motivated murders of Serb, Albanian and Roma civilians.
The defense argued that the senior KLA figures could not control or be held responsible for such acts, as the group lacked a strict command structure.
Lawyers had argued there was no direct evidence linking Thaci's command to any of the alleged crimes.
Seen as heroes in Kosovo

The accused are revered as national heroes in Kosovo, and the KLA and Thaci are seen as symbols of the independence movement. Thaci remained a central political figure after the war and was instrumental in Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence from Serbia.
The verdict in The Hague was livestreamed in the Kosovo capital, Pristina, where thousands of Thaci and KLA supporters gathered.
This follows rallies over the weekend that drew tens of thousands calling for the men's acquittal.
Foreign embassies warned of the possibility of unrest after the verdict.

blocks.caption: KLA supporters rallied in Pristina over the weekendImage: Zana Cimili/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Our war was just, a war of liberation," Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti said ahead of the verdict.
"We believe and hope … that the KLA leaders will return free to their country and to their families," he added.
After being indicted in 2020,Thaci resigned as president and has been detained in The Hague since then.
Tribunal deeply unpopular in Kosovo
Throughout the proceedings, prosecutors tried to distinguish between Kosovo's struggle for independence from Serbia and the alleged crimes committed by the men on trial.

The tribunal responsible for prosecuting the case, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC), was set up in 2016 after earlier cases in Kosovo failed due to alleged political interference and witness intimidation.
Explainer: What are the Kosovo Specialist Chambers?
Although based in The Hague, and staffed by international judges, the KSC was established under Kosovo law specifically to prosecute alleged KLA war crimes.
Nevertheless, the KSC remains deeply unpopular in Kosovo. Out of 15 people indicted so far by the KSC, three are serving sentences.

"Throughout my life, I stood with the people of Kosovo defending freedom, life and dignity. I was always guided by the Western ideals of democracy, equality and justice," Thaci told judges in February as the proceedings concluded.

articles.title: Von der Leyen sets out challenges and opportunities for EU in ‘state of the Union’ speech – Europe live
articles.summary:
European Commission president sets out opportunities and challenges facing the European Union

Von der Leyen frames it as a choice between “independent Europe that stands up…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 3m agoEU's trade relationship with China 'unsustainable' and need to be rebalanced, von der Leyen says
5m ago'We need to electrify Europe,' von der Leyen says, to cut fossil fuel costs down
10m agovon der Leyen warns against anti-European ultranationalists and Russia who 'despise our values'
12m ago'We are now dealing with an openly hostile world,' EU's von der Leyen warns
14m agoEU 'the strongest' but 'most precarious' it has even been, von der Leyen says
36m agoWatch von der Leyen's SOTU live - video
37m agoMorning opening: The state of the European Union

blocks.text: Von der Leyen then turns to investment and growth, as well as the EU’s next budget.
She talks about the need to simplify and tackle fragmentation on investment to help fund European start ups.

She pays specific tribute to the success of ICEYE, a radar satellite imaging and space-based monitoring company, built by Finland’s Pekka Laurila and Poland’s Rafał Modrzewski after they met through Erasmus student exchange programme 15 years ago.
“Today they are one of the world’s leading space technology companies,” she says. “You are a true European success story.”
EU's trade relationship with China 'unsustainable' and need to be rebalanced, von der Leyen says
Von der Leyen turns specifically to China, warning that the EU’s trade deficit with China is now €1bn a day, and it has “reached its tipping point.”

“Some say the second China shock is looming, but it’s already here. It shows in our communities and factories across our union. It leads to deindustrialisation in the industrial heartlands of Europe. This is unsustainable.”
She says the EU “will use all tools at our disposal to rebalance our relationships.”
She also talks about the need to diversify on critical raw materials.
'We need to electrify Europe,' von der Leyen says, to cut fossil fuel costs down
Von der Leyen also talks about the need to reform Europe’s energy market.
She says “Europe cannot remain an industrial powerhouse if its energy prices are structurally too high.”

She says the bloc successfully pivoted towards homegrown cleaner energies in the aftermath of Russia’s full-scale invasion on Ukraine, but it still “bitterly felt the cost” of the strait of Hormuz closing later.

“We need to double down on our affordable and home-grown clean energy. Be it renewables or nuclear, be it biomethane or others. Technologically neutral. But these energies must give us independence and drive down energy prices.”
She says “we need to electrify Europe,” and cut the fossil fuel import bill.
She says lots of renewable capacity is waiting to be connected, and the EU needs to speed up grid connections.
She then turns to trade.
Von der Leyen says “kickstarting Europe’s economy is our number one priority,” as Europe needs to tap into its huge market, world class industries and services.
She says its single market remains too fragmented and needs to reform further, with the aim of completing it by the end of next year.

“In today’s economy, speed is of the essence. A permanent permit or a form, a grid connection of financing decision – all of this can determine where an investment is made and where jobs are created. We need to move much faster,” she says.
Von der Leyen also talks about the need to simplify its rules.
von der Leyen warns against anti-European ultranationalists and Russia who 'despise our values'
Von der Leyen frames it as a choice between “independent Europe that stands up for its values in this world,” or “letting divisions and dependencies hold us back.”

“Do we want to rally around our European idea that together we can decide our own destiny? Or do we let our democracies be undermined by the proxies and puppets of authoritarians? Whether it is the ultra nationalist or the anti-European, whether it’s Russian interference or disinformation, the names may be different, but their goal is the same. They despise our values and they want to shatter our European unity. So let’s not only fight back against that, but let’s fight together for our European ideal.”
'We are now dealing with an openly hostile world,' EU's von der Leyen warns
Von der Leyen warns that “we are now dealing with an openly hostile world,” in which “old assumptions and relationships have frayed.”
She talks about “a territorial war of aggression” in Ukraine, “a fight for industrial capacities” and “narratives,” and “the dizzying speech of change and technology” impacting people’s lives.

“We see this in the rise of the extreme and the decline of nuance, even in the way that we relate to each other. These real concerns are being weaponised to drive a wedge between us, sometimes from the outside, but too often from the inside. But our path is clear. Building an independent Europe that has the power to act. Nothing can divert us from this. Because in this world, the fate of Europe must remain in the hands of Europeans.”
EU 'the strongest' but 'most precarious' it has even been, von der Leyen says
Von der Leyen begins her speech.
She quotes Charles Dickens’s description of the days of the French Revolution, “it was the best of times; it was the worst of times.”
“It is also a fair description of the world we live in,” she says, as she adds “the speed of change is incredible.”

“I would say the state of our union is the strongest it has ever been. The state of our union can also feel as precarious as it has ever been. These two statements may seem incompatible, but they are both true and they reflect these exceptional times.”
She says Europe “has chosen to forge its own path” as it navigates “the complex age of … great possibilities and … great perils.”
Europe is “breaking free from the toxic dependency on Russian fossil fuels,” better prepared to defend itself than ever before, and standing for its values with Ukraine and Greenland, she says.
“In the cold fragility of today’s world, only Europe can provide true sovereignty for Europeans,” she says.
EP’s Metsola sets out what people expect from Europe:

“Our union has always moved forward because people were willing to take a leap where the moment demanded it and turned uncertainty into possibility. People expect a union that does more to protect them, more to support them, and more to fight their corner. They want answers on security, on competitiveness, on affordable homes, on quality jobs, on climate, on borders. They want us to stand up for a Europe of values …”
She goes on, also pointedly mentioning the need to continue supporting Ukraine.
Opening the session, the European parliament president Roberta Metsola welcomes Canada’s Carney, who gets long and warm applause from EU lawmakers.
“They haven’t heard you giving your speech yet,” laughs Metsola.
We are about to start.

blocks.caption: Prime minister Mark Carney participates in a welcoming ceremony with President of the European Parliament Roberta Metsola and President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: It’s also worth noting that this year’s SOTU will see a special guests in attendance: Canada’s prime minister Mark Carney.

blocks.caption: Canadian prime minister Mark Carney is welcomed by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and Roberta Metsola, President of the European Parliament. Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters

blocks.text: He will listen to von der Leyen’s speech as Canada seeks closer ties with the EU – particularly on defence, digital regulation and trade - amid growing tensions with and outright repeated threats from US president Donald Trump.
Carney will also address the European parliament on Thursday.
Watch von der Leyen's SOTU live - video
The speech is expected to start in the next 10-15 minutes, so you can watch as the European Parliament’s Hemicycle in Strasbourg is filling up ahead of the speech.
Here’s our live stream for today:
Morning opening: The state of the European Union

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

The European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is about to speak at the European parliament to discuss “the state of the Union” in her annual speech about the EU’s place in the ever more complicated world.

blocks.caption: A light illumination on a wall at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France. Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPA

blocks.text: Her speech in Strasbourg comes as the list of challenges facing the bloc grows ever longer – not least an increasingly aggressive Russia following incidents involving Denmark, Lithuania, and Poland this week. Security is set to be a key theme.

We are also likely to hear about Europe’s competitiveness and its standing in a global race dominated by superpowers like China and the US, as well as the rise of nationalism and populism across the continent and beyond.

Expect updates on other major priorities, too: digital regulation (with a sharp focus on online safety), migration (following the Ceuta crisis in late July), and climate and energy in the wake of another record-breaking summer.
Plenty to cover. I will bring you all the key lines here.
It’s Wednesday, 16 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: ‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South Africa
articles.summary:
String of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week

The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s…

blocks.text: The discovery of the bodies of seven women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide.

When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral.

Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising.

On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in Olifantsfontein, about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed.
“In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo.

blocks.caption: Elizabeth Moselakgomo was abducted and killed while out for a run on 9 September.

blocks.text: South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. In the year to 31 March 2024, more than 27,600 people were murdered, 5,578 of them women, according to the latest police data.

For years, women have called on the South African government to take gender-based violence seriously. After hundreds of women protested on the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis.
However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed.

The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.”

South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy group Women For Change.
“It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said.

Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe, told reporters: “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.”
Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody.
Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations.
Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A protest against femicide in Johannesburg last November. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates for women in the world. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: “When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of Sonke Gender Justice.

“You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.”
The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief.
Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays.
“She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’.
“That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.”
Running clubs around South Africa organised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women.

She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.”

articles.title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms
articles.summary: Sam Altman and other tech CEOs say there are incentives to limit advancements in AI, as fears grow over the threats it poses to humanity.

blocks.text: The boss of ChatGPT maker Open AI says people should have more faith in his firm and others like it to do the right thing when it comes to artificial intelligence (AI) development amid rising public concerns about the risks.
"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.
However, Altman noted that people were justified in their fears around AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.
Speaking in Washington meanwhile, left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon have both called for greater governance of AI.
Altman's comments came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce.
"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."

It was the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could kill all humans by the end of the decade if left unchecked.

A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.

The fervour over the claims has led to more scrutiny of AI development in recent days, and in response, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called for the pace of all AI development to slow, external and urged governments to regulate the industry.
The post was applauded by Altman, as well as co-founder of Google's DeepMind Demis Hassabis, and Elon Musk, owner of social media site X and AI assistant Grok.
By Tuesday, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement.
Altman said that he felt AI companies like his own were capable of essentially regulating themselves.

"We will get it right, I'm very confident in our company's and industry's ability to do this safely," Altman said, adding that he was sure that they would "keep alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" and if they couldn't, they would "slow down or stop".
Despite the assurances, political figures have cautioned against self-regulation.

Bernie Sanders, an independent senator from Vermont who votes with the Democrats, said decisions over AI's development have been made by "a handful of the richest people in the world", naming Elon Musk, Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, among others.
Speaking at a conference hosted in Washington, he said: "The people of this country must make the decisions about AI, and not just a handful of oligarchs."
Bannon, who served as a White House strategist during Trump's first term, also cast doubt on the tech industry's ability to self regulate.
"We can never trust what an oligarch says because... they're disingenuous and they lie," Bannon said at the same conference.
After Altman's comments, Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X that every AI lab has the ability and the incentive "to take its own actions" towards making AI tools and models that are designed for safety.
"Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," Zuckerberg wrote. "Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well."
Jensen Huang, head of Nvidia, also said at the same Tuesday conference that the AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released and not be managed by outside forces.
"We don't need new laws or regulations," Huang said, adding that there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products.
Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for the AI computing chips it makes.
"Safety is paramount. However, safety is an engineering problem," Huang said.
He added that if at any time a leader of an AI company lacks confidence in their product they should choose to not release it.
"That's a very obvious thing to do," Huang said. "Run as fast as you can, but if at any time you feel the institution is not in control, take a pause."
Some industry figures have argued resurgent AI fears were overblown and were being jumped on to generate hype for the industry.

During the conference, Altman addressed a crowd of hundreds of business people, telling them they should use AI tools to aid in their work, but also needed them in order to protect their businesses from potentially AI-enabled cyber attacks.
The idea of AI executives being left to entirely regulate themselves has struck some in the industry as a bad idea.
Jack Clark, an Anthropic executive and co-founder, told the BBC on Monday that leaving AI to be a "totally unregulated industry" was "rolling dice with immense risks".

Patrick Hillman, the chief operating officer of Logical Intelligence, which is chaired by Yann LeCun, a sage of the AI industry, noted Tuesday how little faith people have in tech companies to do anything truly in the public interest, external.
"The only institution that Americans might trust less than Washington these days is Silicon Valley. I have worked and lived in both and I assure you both have earned this scepticism," Hillman said.
"If you believe what you are building is dangerous, show us what you are prepared to stop doing," he added.
Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety.

Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development.
He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact.
"We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said.

OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs, external "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind.
"With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote.
